the next item on the agenda is the debate on the report of mr norbert lins and mr bart staes, on behalf of the special committee on the union pesticide authorisation procedure, on the union pesticide authorisation procedure (2018/2153 (ini)) (a8-0475/2018).
member of the commission. – mr president, yes, of course, european citizens expect safe and healthy food – and rightly so. however, while ensuring food safety remains an imperative, it is no longer sufficient in itself. increasingly, citizens have concerns about how their food is produced, about the sustainability of the food system and about environmental protection. we can only meet these expectations if we come together, learn lessons from recent challenges and move forward in the interests of all citizens. in this context, i would like to thank your house for having set up this excellent special committee on the union’s authorisation procedure for pesticides (pest) last year, notably following the commission’s report on the implementation of the directive on the sustainable use of pesticides, the european citizens’ initiative and the debate on glyphosate. the committee’s work is very important as we all aim to ensure transparency and an evidence—based food safety system, dispelling any doubts european citizens may have as to the neutrality of science, because the main challenge is how we can we guarantee that the science is excellent, perfect and neutral, and not biased. so i am pleased to have this opportunity to discuss the pest committee’s report with you today. this special committee was set up in december 2017, following the renewal of glyphosate’s approval for a further five years. its mandate was to analyse the current eu system of approval for active substances and authorisation of plant protection products. it was also asked to identify areas for possible improvements. one of the key outcomes of the pest committee’s assessment is the need to restore trust in the eu system, in particular trust in the scientific evaluation of a substance and trust in the risk management phase. a high level of transparency is critical to this: firstly, making all studies used as a basis for risk assessment publicly available, and, secondly, the utmost transparency on discussions and positions held in the regulatory committee which decides which active substances to approve. i think that it is safe to say that we have come a long way since last year. the commission’s proposal of april 2018 on the transparency and sustainability of eu risk assessment in the food chain aims to rebuild trust in the system. it addresses many of the pest committee’s recommendations, notably, firstly, transparency during risk assessment, secondly, the quality and reliability of studies, and, thirdly, improving risk communication. as i already stressed last december during our debate on the proposal for a revision of the general food law, european citizens have expressed in recent years such a clear and repeated demand for more transparency in the way risk assessments are conducted and i have been carefully listening to them and active since the beginning of my mandate on this issue. i have also carefully read the resolution on glyphosate that you voted on a year ago, where you stressed that the european union’s authorisation procedure, including the scientific evaluation of substances, should be based only on published studies. i believe that it is through greater transparency that we will increase the confidence of citizens in the risk assessment system. transparency can help us to avoid potential bias in science. it is crucial to improve trust in the eu evidence-based food safety system and in science in general. i am confident that, when adopted, this proposal will greatly help in this respect. on this proposal, i thank you once again for your plenary vote last month and for the constructive first trilogue, which i am pleased took place this afternoon. given the importance of this issue for european citizens, i know you will work actively to make progress in the discussions with the council to allow an agreement to be found in this legislative term. you can, of course, count on me and my services to work energetically with you to achieve this objective in our role as an honest broker, and i know that dg sante and the pest committee have had a very good collaboration in the whole period of building this report. this would allow the new regulation to apply as soon as possible, including in the pesticides sector. but, even before this proposal, in the area of pesticides, i had taken a number of steps to increase citizens’ trust in the decision-making and risk management process. for the most sensitive files, such as glyphosate, neonicotinoids and endocrine disruptors, the commission now has dedicated websites. these sites list all the different versions of the draft proposals and detailed minutes of the discussions held with member states. equally, the commission receives a high number of requests for access to documents on pesticides. since last april, all documents to which access is given have been made publicly available. in addition, with the proposal revising the comitology regulation, the commission aims to increase voting transparency at the appeal committee level, making the votes of member states’ representatives public. in its report, the pest committee rightly notes that the eu has one of the most stringent systems in the world to regulate pesticides, but that, of course, it needs to be improved. i agree. there is no such thing as a perfect system. it is always possible to improve procedures to approve active substances and authorisations of plant protection products. with this in mind, we are currently carrying out a regulatory fitness and performance programme (refit) to evaluate our pesticide legislation. this includes both the regulation on plant protection products and the regulation on pesticide residues and will soon be finalised. its objective is to identify areas where improvements are needed. i want to take this opportunity to welcome the parliament’s focus on this issue. in addition to the pest committee’s forthcoming report, the member of the european parliament, pavel poc, has also examined the implementation of the plant protection regulation and the parliament’s research services have already produced a study on this topic. we also have the scientific advice mechanism’s (sam) opinion on pesticides and the findings of the audits conducted by the commission services in the member states. please be assured that all of these outputs will feed into the commission’s analysis as we move ahead, and the pest committee report will provide valuable input for this exercise. while improvements within the current legal framework can be put in place swiftly, given the timing it will be for the next commission to decide whether to propose changes to the legislation that ultimately would have to be adopted by the parliament and council. to conclude, i would like to stress that we all share the same goal: to maintain food safety, protect citizens’, animals’ and plants’ health, and to safeguard the environment. i want to thank you once again for the pest committee’s engagement and the valuable work undertaken by the pest committee and your house. in particular, i would to thank the chair, mr andrieu, the vice-chairs, the co-rapporteurs, mr lins and mr staes, as well as the shadow rapporteurs. i look forward to the final adoption of the report on wednesday and i assure you once again that all your precise, detailed and specific conclusions will be duly taken on board. we will continue to work tirelessly on increasing transparency, building trust and improving the sustainability of our food safety system. the commission will assess carefully the final conclusions and recommendations in the context of its refit evaluation of the pesticides legislation.
on behalf of the ppe group mr president, commissioner, first of all i would like to congratulate the two rapporteurs on the great work they have done and you, commissioner, on your involvement in these sensitive issues. we have been working in committee for months, listening to the experts and analysing the procedures for the authorisation of pesticides, both community and member state. i understand and share the objectives of transparency, of ensuring the level of protection of human health, of increasing consumer confidence or reducing administrative burdens. however, we must avoid any further questioning of the results of scientific opinions on the basis of ideological factors which affect the capacity for innovation and competitiveness. the increasing media coverage of decision-making on pesticide use requires that this debate be brought back to the technical and scientific level. decisions on pesticides must be made solely and exclusively on the basis of scientific criteria, without political or ideological interference. i would like to remind you - as the contact person for parliament and efsa - that this agency is independent and scientifically sound, and that its work is exclusively subject to the regulation in force. but it must not be forgotten that the procedure used by the union to authorise plant protection products is one of the strictest in the world. the fact is that there is no such thing as zero risk, and the use of these products also involves risks, which can always be minimised; and i am talking about doses, the time of application or the application procedure. finally, commissioner, i think it would be very interesting if the commission prepared a communication to discuss and debate the revision of legislation on plant protection products, in order to unify criteria and standardize risk analysis procedures. i think this is very necessary.
madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, we are discussing measures to ensure the health of citizens, and that health is ensured by controlling the environment and food. it is important that we ensure that plant protection products are used correctly and that they have the desired effect on health and the environment. we must also help to ensure that fruit and vegetables can continue to be produced in the european union. i think we can all agree on this, but to ban for the sake of banning is neither wise nor logical. we must make decisions based on scientific criteria. our institutions, with efsa at the forefront, are in a position to provide information, to offer transparency, security and certainty to european citizens. let us therefore leave the scientists to their work and, from the political point of view, let us ensure that there are the means for them to continue their work without politicizing science, because we will not be doing the citizens any favors if we offer them ideological messages and distorted opinions instead of scientific certainty, as in the case of glyphosate. that is what i want to say to you today, in addition to thanking you for your work, especially my colleague mr lins, who i know has done a very thorough job and a great deal of effort with this document.

the rapporteur. madam president, i would like to begin by paying tribute - before i go into the matter - to pawel adamowicz - the mayor of gdansk, who has just been killed as a result of the attack he suffered yesterday - a true defender of rights and freedoms in this europe threatened by the emergence of dark forces. his murder is a european tragedy, and i want to begin my speech today by paying tribute to him and saying that his fight for freedom and rights is the fight, and will continue to be the fight, of everyone. i would also like to begin by expressing my gratitude to marisa matias for the preparation of this report, as well as to the teams that have made it possible for us to have, for the first time, put a central issue, such as taxation, at the heart of gender equality policies. we cannot go one more minute into such a fundamental area, which defines our model of well-being and our resources and how we deal with, how we collect and how we spend our resources, without this being done without any kind of gender perspective. and it's important because it allows us to go on the offensive on a gender equality agenda that needs to be extremely ambitious. i have to say that in the four years that i've been here we've had an extremely timid equality agenda. most of the directives on equality are stalled in the council, whether it is the directive on the representation of women on boards of directors, or the whole process we had to go through with the withdrawal of the directive on maternity leave, and also the difficulties we are having with the ratification of the istanbul convention. we've had an extremely shy legislature on equality. and we have to be aware that, at this moment, there are forces that are emerging in a brutal way at the level of the european union, that are calling into question fundamental principles, such as, for example, that there is gender violence, by political formations that are getting a lot of votes in the european union, as, for example, we have just seen recently in andalusia. and, by the way, i would like to congratulate all those who will be taking to the streets in spain tomorrow - in solidarity with the andalusian women - following the aberrant agreement that has been reached, which is also a real disgrace to the equality of people because of the participation of that party. but these forces are putting the foundations in question. we cannot go back to debating whether or not there is gender-based violence. we need to go on the offensive, with a gender equality agenda that is really ambitious, fighting violence, fighting wage inequality and including new forms of discrimination that have never been addressed before. for example, taxation, which is the subject of this report. and so, starting to have public policies that look at how our tax systems, both in direct and indirect taxation, tackle inequality is very important. and this report, for example, if we talk about the question of direct taxation, it states how in many member states of the european union we have seen that the obligation to do so, the possibility of taxing joint income discourages the second supplier of that declaration from entering the labour market. and that is direct discrimination which encourages women to have difficulty in accessing the labour market. or, if we talk about indirect taxation - and this has been pointed out by many movements in many countries, in france and elsewhere - how is it that, at the moment, products which are women's basic necessities are loaded with a luxury vat? this is absolutely intolerable. and also, another of the things that report points out, which is very important. we have to look at the different consumption patterns between men and women. and if you look at them, it is very clear that women are now paying more vat on average than men. so neither the european semester nor all the debates we are having on taxation, which have been very important in this mandate, can continue to be absolutely blind to the issue of gender equality and taxation. and so this report, and i end with this, calls for us to tackle this phenomenon in an ambitious way now and, above all, in the next legislature, and to recover that ambitious and courageous gender equality agenda which is what the european union needs.

president-in-office of the council. – madam president, the migratory situation in the mediterranean sea has improved significantly over the last years in terms of the number of arrivals. in total in 2018, approximately 150 000 irregular arrivals were registered at our external borders in the mediterranean. this represents a fall by a quarter compared with 2017 and is the lowest level in five years. this total for 2018 was also 92% below the peak of the migratory crisis in 2015. this shows that our resolute and comprehensive action and our engagement with key partner countries have paid off and should continue to be pursued. the number of deaths at sea remains too high, of course, and efforts must continue to bring it down. but in 2018 this number also decreased by a quarter since 2017, and on the central mediterranean route alone, the decrease is more than 50%. the unhcr estimates that in 2018 the libyan coast guard rescued or intercepted nearly 50 000 migrants at sea. the eu holds an important stake in that number, and i would do like to start by referring to recent developments regarding libya and the eu emergency trust fund for africa. since 2014, the european union has mobilised eur 338 million on migration-related projects in libya, eur 318 million under the eu emergency trust fund for africa, and eur 20 million as bilateral assistance. one third – eur 91 million – was granted to support the libyan coast guard in the form of training, including on human rights and equipment to set up basic operational rooms for the coast guard in tripoli and to support the development of libya’s own maritime rescue coordination centre. eunavfor operation sophia has so far provided training for a total of 237 coast guard personnel, and the european asylum support office (easo) has provided training on access to the asylum procedure. regarding our support inland in libya, an important component of the eu emergency trust fund programme consists of eur 134.7 million in assistance and protection services to stranded migrants. it also covers voluntary humanitarian return assistance by the international organization for migration (iom), including reintegration support, which has benefited over 16 000 migrants in 2018 and over 19 000 migrants in 2017. the eu entirely supports the evacuation of asylum seekers and refugees from libya in the framework of the evacuation transit mechanism (etm) by unhcr. since its start in 2017, this has so far benefited over 2 800 persons. finally, on 4 december 2018, following a month of negotiations with the authorities, the unhcr – again with eu support – was able to open a gathering and departure facility in tripoli. the facility is the first open centre in libya, hosting migrants released from detention centres in view of resettlement. nevertheless, a number of challenges remain on all mediterranean routes, and they are very different from one another. the european council conclusions of june last year set out clear guidance for priority action on each route. hence we will continue taking forward the implementation of existing policies on the eastern and central mediterranean routes. on the eastern mediterranean route, numbers remain low, but the significant increase of irregular arrivals at the greek-turkish land border shows that we must keep a vigilant attitude to any shifts along the route. in this respect, cooperation with turkey under the eu—turkey statement, as well as with our western balkan partners, is essential. our work with neighbouring mediterranean countries on the more pressing issues has been complimented with further engagement with countries further afield in africa. the regional dialogue in recent years, the rabat and khartoum processes and the valletta action plan represent useful frameworks for a comprehensive and deep cooperation with african partners. they are supplemented by a robust set of funding instruments, including the eu emergency trust fund for africa, through which the eu has been able to mobilise more than eur 4 billion for actions across the main african migratory routes. new cooperation initiatives are also in the pipeline, like the upcoming eu—au ministerial meeting of 21—22 january 2019, which will contribute to strengthening region—to—region ties and addressing common challenges. it will also establish a regular forum for discussions with our african partners. regarding the reform of the eu asylum rules, the council has worked intensively on these complex files during successive presidencies. fruitful negotiations have taken place between the council and the european parliament, which resulted in substantial progress on five of the seven proposals. the romanian presidency stands ready to continue these efforts in order to make progress where possible. for other important legislative files, like the schengen borders code, the visa code and the immigration liaison officers regulation, the presidency hopes to conclude the ongoing trilogues with parliament before the elections. regarding the reform of the european border and coast guard, both co—legislators are putting a lot of effort into reaching a position which will allow them to start interinstitutional negotiations. however, there are still significant disagreements between member states on some major issues of the asylum reform, in particular the dublin regulation. while all member states agree on the importance of striking the right balance between responsibility and solidarity, it has so far proved impossible to find a compromise on the concrete elements of that balance. it has been argued that enhancing the responsibilities of member states should be compensated by a predictable system which is capable of providing relief to frontline member states faced with a crisis. striking the right balance is not only about finding the right formula for the distribution mechanism. solidarity can be expressed in different ways. the complexity of the situation is demonstrated by the fact that, notwithstanding the important decrease in the number of arrivals, there is still a high number of asylum applications, a big proportion of which are lodged in countries other than the frontline member states. this shows that there are significant secondary movements which will need to be tackled if we want to come to a structural solution for the issue at stake.

union’s asylum rules, now is the time for the governments to take up their responsibilities in the council and stop blaming the commission. on behalf of the ppe group madam president, although the mediterranean crisis has brought attention to immediate needs, it has also highlighted the structural limitations of the union's migration policy tools. in 2016, the commission launched seven proposals to reform the common european asylum system. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. the instruments contained in these proposals represent, even on their own, a step forward in migration management. the reform of the 'eurodac' system, the regulation for the european asylum support office or the creation of a common resettlement framework can go ahead if there is political will and political agreement, but further work on the reform of the dublin system is necessary as, two years after the commission launched its proposal, divergent positions among member states persist and have prevented the council from adopting a mandate to open negotiations with parliament. the union has everything in its power to alleviate this crisis: the european agenda on migration 2015, the emergency trust fund for africa or the union's external investment plan. in addition to the seven legislative proposals, a budget increase is planned for the next financial framework which could reach eur 10 billion, not forgetting the signing of the global compact on migration with the united nations. but solidarity and better management are needed to prevent men, women and children fleeing terror, war or climate change from becoming homeless, dying at sea or falling into the hands of criminal networks. the adoption of the seven reports and a firm commitment to european solidarity in the face of selfish resistance and short-sighted policies would be a good solution.
madam president, first of all i would like to say to the romanian presidency that you have one last chance to try to shed some light on this serious problem we are facing in the european union. it will be difficult for you to do worse than the austrian presidency, so you have a chance. because it is very frustrating to have to discuss this issue again in this parliament. this is a parliament and it is there for that, but the citizens of europe must know that this parliament has done its duty; that we have a road map to solve the grave humanitarian crisis in the mediterranean and in africa; that we have a recipe for reforming the dublin system in an efficient and humane way; and that it is the governments, many governments of the member states, that are holding back that solution. it is very important that the citizens know this, because the citizens speak for the european union as a whole. and it's not the whole of the european union. this parliament has done its job, the commission is doing, to a large extent, its job, and it is the council that is blocking a solution. we talk about this mediterranean problem as if it were a humanitarian tragedy. that's what our headline says, but we treat it as if it were a mere technical problem. and we have 49 people stranded by winter storms because we're unable to accommodate them in one of our ports. and that's because there are governments in the european union that are blocking a common asylum and migration policy. this is what the citizens need to know. so that they can address their governments as well. because, i repeat, this parliament, which is also made up of 27 different nationalities and very different political groups, has managed to vote for an important agreement which would provide a solution to the current plight of refugees and migrants. we did our job. it is your turn, ladies and gentlemen of the council.

mr. president, allow me to abuse just one second of your generosity. we have had a debate to celebrate the 20th anniversary of the euro - a successful project - but i want to draw attention to the fact that the six people who have spoken about the success of this project, about its benefits, have been men. i hope it will not take another 20 years before women are properly integrated.
the rapporteur. mr president, welcome to the house, mr draghi. as always, it's a pleasure to have you in this house. and i would like to begin by thanking the rapporteurs and all the colleagues for their great support and cooperation in presenting what i consider to be a good report. the euro has turned 20 years old, and at the height of its popularity. three out of four citizens think it's good for our economy. what started as the common currency for 11 countries is now the common currency for 19.3 billion people. and, furthermore, the euro is coming up on its 20th anniversary after a great year. in 2017, the european economy grew at its strongest pace in the last ten years. but more importantly, all member states saw their economies expand. and we must recognize that this is due both to the monetary policy of the european central bank and to the structural reforms that have been carried out in many member states. the latest data published by eurostat in july last year show us that we are moving in the right direction. economic growth for 2018 and 2019 is consolidated above 2%. unemployment is basically at pre-crisis levels of around 7%, while the number of people in employment and the euro area labour market participation ratio are at their highest levels since the creation of monetary and economic union in 1999. but not everything is positive. i am alarmed by the lack of upward convergence and the tendency of some member states not to address their structural deficits. as regards inflation, the european central bank, whose statutory independence is fundamental, and i repeat, is fulfilling its mandate to keep inflation below, but around 2%. in the medium term, inflation is expected to remain at around 1,7% in 2018, 2019 and 2020, and this is undoubtedly thanks to the measures taken. we have also seen an improvement in credit to the private sector, which, by mid-2018, was increasing at a rate of 3% per annum. that said, we have to be cautious because of the uncertainty that is emerging around the european union with the resurgence of populisms, negotiations and possible consequences of brexit and protectionism, among many other risks. we must concentrate our efforts on the essential, which is to ensure that we remain on the path of economic growth and job creation, which is the real social policy. the key to this is to maintain a favourable environment for public and private investment, bringing it back to its pre-crisis levels. in this respect, further action by the ecb is needed to ensure that its monetary policy achieves the objective of restoring credit to the real economy, particularly to smes, which are the backbone of our economy, and that monetary accommodation measures benefit society as a whole. in the report we have prepared and which we shall be voting on tomorrow, we have covered all the aspects of the monetary policy of the european central bank, giving an assessment of the measures which had to be taken, but also welcoming the decision to reduce these measures gradually, as long as the economic situation allows it. we highlight the potential rise in interest rates, the reduction of the asset purchase programme, liquidity auctions, the launch of the corporate bond purchase programme and, of course, the public debt purchase programme in the euro area. but i would like to stress that the european central bank cannot solve the structural problems of the member states. it is up to the member states, in cooperation with the european institutions, to act at national level to establish a solid foundation on which to build the european union. the ecb's measures are transitional in nature and their main advantage is that they give member states time to consolidate their fiscal position and implement structural reforms which will create the conditions for continuing on the path of economic growth, something in which we are all involved.
on behalf of the green group, mr president, the european central bank, with its unconventional measures, has kept the economy of a very unreasonably designed eurozone afloat. there are some things about those measures that you have to look at, elements of democratization. also, as president draghi knows, we are concerned about the purchase of carbon-related assets, which do not contribute to the fight against climate change. but these measures have kept the european economy afloat. the question now is whether we will be able to make the reforms we know the eurozone needs to avoid future crises. and we are concerned that there is a strange coalition between those who do not want to reduce risks and those who do not want to mutualise them that prevents that reform from actually happening. we must move towards automatic stabilizers; we must move towards countercyclical mechanisms at the level of the european union, with a budget of this name. without this, the weaknesses of the euro in the future will remain very great, and it is therefore essential to take this leap which, without a doubt, the euro must take after its creation, twenty years ago.
vice-president of the commission. – mr president, in my introductory remarks i recalled the constructive engagement that has developed between the european parliament and the european central bank over the past years, and the large convergence of views in many aspects of mr mato’s report shows that this continues to be the case. however, in my concluding remarks let me come back to a point which was also highlighted in the report: the need for financial integration, amongst others things, to improve the transmission of a monetary policy. and this brings me to the topic of the capital markets union and completion of the banking union. but there i would point out that out of the 30 legislative proposals which the commission has put out on the capital markets union, only three proposals have been adopted, and there is political agreement on a further two. so, therefore, we count on your continued support for the capital markets union project, which would lead to deeper and better-connected capital markets and thus also foster the international standing of the euro.
president of the european central bank. – mr president, first of all, i thank the rapporteur, honourable member, mr mato, for his report. i certainly thank you for all the compliments the ecb has received and i will respond to the criticisms. first of all, about the european deposit insurance scheme (edis). the ecb has always been a supporter of edis, of the insurance. i want just to make three points about that. first of all, whatever the road is to edis, the final goal of having a fully mutualised edis should always remain in sight. now the road to that goal is not going to be simple, we all know that. and so various steps and delays and compromises and negotiations are necessary. but the direction and the sense of final results should always be present. so what you decide about how to move ahead, will be really in your own judgment. the important thing is that, whatever you decide, we’ll never compromise over the final outcome. the third point i want to make about edis is that there is no clear progress on this road unless there is convincing risk reduction everywhere. by the way, big progress has been achieved on that front already but more needs to be done. the ecb has shown in various places on various occasions that risk sharing also itself contributes to risk reduction, so the two arms of this journey towards the final goal of a fully—neutralised insurance system should go hand in hand. several questions addressed the economic effects of the policy of the ecb. comparisons were made with non—euro parts of the world and with before the euro – how the world was beautiful, fantastic, before the euro. i’ve gone through these comparisons in a recent speech i gave. it was not fantastic, especially for the countries that complain most today about the euro; it was not fantastic at all before the euro. let me make a comparison with the united states, because someone raised that point. the employment rate in 1998 in the euro area at 19 was 59.8%, now it’s 67.3% – the highest ever in the euro area. in the united states, it was 73.9% in 1998, today it’s 70.6% so it went down, not up. the jobs created in the euro area over this period of time have been 19.8 million. and the jobs created in the united states were 17.2 million. of course we have to be careful about making these comparisons because the units have to be standardised and the same thing we get on the employment numbers, in millions. so when i’m asked about the side effects of our monetary policy in the euro area, the response is that the main side effect between 2013 – when the situation was at its worst – and today, has been the creation of 9.6 million jobs, which is more than ever. that’s the main side effect. other questions related to the presence of financial stability risks. well, it’s true that in certain localised areas over the euro area we observed that valuations are stretched in prime commercial real estate. also in some areas of some countries in the residential real estate, in some segments of the bond market. but are any of these risks prone to generate systemic financial stability risk? the answer that we give so far is no. but of course we monitor all this very carefully. and the answer to these local situations cannot be a change in monetary policy. it has to be the use of macroprudential tools by the national governments. we’ve said this and, in fact, national governments have indeed responded, with their national instruments together with the ecb. more generally, some questions addressed the role of the ecb and very rightly, as observed by the rapporteur, the ecb has its role but cannot fill all the roles that everybody else should fill. the ecb has a role which is limited to monetary policy, which is circumscribed by its mandate. it cannot do everybody else’s job. in this sense, as i have said on a variety of occasions including this morning, not all its benefits have accrued to all the members of the euro area. why is that? because of two main reasons. reforms are necessary in these countries whether they belong to the euro, or are outside the euro. you have got to make the reforms that are necessary. there is not a blueprint which is the same for all countries. it does change from country to country; each country has its own history. and so that’s the basic thing: no reforms, no growth. but then there are also problems, also incompleteness in the economic and monetary union. and the first incompleteness is to finish the things that had been decided already, namely the banking union. the second is to start to move fast on the capital markets union and the third is to build fiscal capacity. but if you do the first two things – and the european parliament has really carried out a very positive and constructive role at each and every point in time of this discussion – if these two things are done, we are way better, even if the next steps on the creation of the fiscal capacity may take longer for pretty obvious political difficulties. there was one question about what the ecb could do about certain specific loans that banks have lent to citizens. generally, the ecb cannot do anything about that, it’s the national competent authority. very often, these issues are a consumer protection issue, so it’s the national consumer protection authority that has to monitor the conditions of lending. but generally speaking – and this holds true also in other countries where the non—performing loans (npls) problem is really very dramatic because of its social consequences – in non—performing loans you always have two types of debtors: the ones who are normal or even strategic debtors and the ones who are part of a big social problem. for these problems, the response is not to change the payments culture but rather to help the poor people who cannot pay back. one should keep the two things separate. don’t change, don’t affect, don’t damage, don’t harm your banking system, your financial system because the result of this will only be that they will not be able to lend as much as they could to the private sector of your economy, but rather help the poor people who cannot pay. now, one question that has been asked from several sides is if we are heading towards the next recession – and i will say something about that in a moment – does the ecb have the tools to address this? the answer is yes. the ecb has the tools to address this but keep in mind that our present monetary policy stance is very accommodative already. we have negative interest rates and they are expected to be like this for an extended period of time. and, even though we have decided to stop the net asset purchases, we also decided that the current stock will stay what it is for a considerable period of time. what does it mean? it means that, as bonds come to maturity, we repurchase the bonds. what does it mean in terms of numbers? it means that we will continue buying, by and large – at least this year or the next year – 15 billion euros of bonds a month, which was, by and large, what we had been buying in the last 3 months of last year. there was perhaps more than one question about whether our monetary policy has helped equity. we went into some depth in trying to understand what the effects are of monetary policy on the distribution of income, distribution of wealth. it’s quite clear that each monetary policy decision has distributional effects. when we change interest rates we change distribution between creditors and debtors, or between young and old. but certainly the asset purchases, the quantitative easing (qe), have distributional impacts which are even more visible and direct because asset prices go up and the owners of assets are usually the wealthy ones. so the question we ask ourselves is, is our policy worsening the distribution? if you consider all the effects, the answer is no. why is that? it is true that it worsens the distribution in the short term. however, what is the factor that worsens the distribution more than any other factor? it’s the unemployment. where the monetary policy of the ecb has been a success was in fostering strong employment growth, as i presented at the beginning of this response. one question addressed the point of access by smes to credit. has our policy prevented, restrained, or shrunk access by smes to credit? the answer is absolutely no. both our corporate bond programme and our qe programme created space in the bank’s balance sheet for lending more to the smes. all data since 2013, since even when we started with the longer—term refinancing operations (ltros) – by the way the ltros are not unconditional lending – and the targeted longer—term refinancing operations (tltros), is lending to banks on condition they lend to firms, to the real economy. i don’t know where the fairy tale thing about eur 29 out of a hundred actually came from. in terms of another interesting irony of some of the questions, was that one hears that monetary financing of the deficit is now the solution to all problems. that’s one of the questions that was raised before. that is actually interesting. first of all, because when monetary financing was available, for the countries that actually vastly used monetary financing before the euro, the situation was very bad. they got very high inflation and they got unemployment higher than countries that did not use monetary financing. what is actually quite paradoxical is that you hear this solution of monetary financing from people who were against monetary financing as an utmost crime until yesterday. i think i have responded to most of the problems, and now one word about the outlook. if we take a snapshot of the situation as it is today, statically, we still see a situation where consumption is still expanding, relatively strong, investment still expanding, supported by our monetary policy, export growth is less, but still good. and the labour market keeps on being very strong. however, all this is happening at lower and lower growth rates. and we have been receiving weaker data than expected now for a longer time than we had expected a few months ago. in other words, at the beginning we had lower data and we said – and we continue to say, by the way – that some of this weaker momentum was due to temporary factors, and specific to sectors and certain countries. for example, what happened to the car industry; this is one example which is a temporary drop. but then we also said that there are also some more permanent causes of this slowing—down. and the causes of this slowing—down are going to stay. one of which is simply that 2017 was a pretty exceptional year when compared with historical averages. and so we return to a lower growth path. but then the question that we should ask is, first of all, is this what is called a sag or is it heading towards a recession? and the answer we give is no, it’s a slowdown, which is not heading towards a recession, but it could be longer than was expected before. and on what does the length of this slowdown depend? to answer this question we have to go back and ask ourselves what are the factors that originally caused this weakening in growth. and the factors deal primarily with some slowdown in china, of course, but with what we call geopolitical uncertainties. and here, the natural question to ask is how long will these geopolitical uncertainties last. these geopolitical uncertainties put into question the pillars upon which the order, that was built after the second world war, was constructed. and they put into question the european union. they have to do with brexit. they have to do with trade tensions with china. they have to do with the denial of the multilateral system. and we notice, however, that some of these things get better and some others get worse. the result of this, however, is that, at least for some time to come, there’s going to be a continuing uncertainty that changes nature, and this has a cost. and the cost is lower confidence – lower business confidence and lower consumer confidence. that’s why we are now assessing the situation, as i said. my impression is, mr president, that i have responded to all questions. if i missed someone i apologise.
the rapporteur. mr president, i would like to reiterate to you, mr draghi, that i am glad you are here, even if today has resulted in you becoming almost more of an audience than an analysis of the 2017 annual report. but it sounds good. and i would like to thank you, of course, for your recognition of the work that this parliament is doing. may he follow his example! i would also like to thank vice-president dombrovskis for his positive analysis of the report. and of course, thanks to the colleagues who have intervened. even those whose positions i do not share. i agree with mr draghi that we must not be complacent and that we must strengthen our capacity to adapt and equip ourselves with the instruments to face new crises. we already have crisis experience. we don't make the same mistakes. it is true that we have a stronger monetary union, but there are still some unresolved issues. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. i also agree that risk reduction and risk sharing must go hand in hand. and that's the end of it. i want to remind you of the importance of not settling and moving forward. i would therefore like to highlight two points which have been taken up in the report with the almost unanimous support of this parliament: the importance of continuing to move towards greater financial integration through the capital markets union, which will help the smooth transmission of monetary policy and ensure greater stability in the euro area; the need to meet the sustainability objectives in the context of monetary policies - the ecb is under the paris agreement and, like all the european institutions, has to support the achievement of the objectives set; and finally, i would like to acknowledge something which has also been highlighted by mr draghi: the work done by the ecb on transparency to improve the communication of its policies, especially given that the ecb has absolute independence in the conduct of its monetary policy, and as it is enshrined in the treaties. the triangle of accountability, greater transparency and independence is key.
on behalf of the s&d group. mr president, thank you very much, mr vice-president of the commission, for being here. first of all, i must thank mr nils torvalds, as rapporteur for this report, for his spirit of collaboration and the other rapporteurs for the effort we have made to reach this agreement, this text of agreement which we are voting on tomorrow. in any case, i would like to point out that these reports in which we assess the functioning of the banking union are timely, they are necessary, but it is key to be able to complete the institutional framework of the banking union at once. this parliament has made a great effort in this legislature and especially in recent months to deal with the risk reduction packages - the banking package, the regulations to regulate bad loans - but we need an additional effort in these last months to be able to finish designing a deposit insurance for the whole of the banking union, to secure a product - that public debt securitisation - that is a safe public bond and also a safeguard mechanism, a backstop, for the single resolution fund. we have taken steps, as i said, to reduce the risks, but we still have to take steps to share them. and that is why i dare to ask this parliament to be able to take advantage of these four months, to be able to negotiate as much as we can to finish having that deposit insurance, those other instruments so necessary for the banking union to work and not have to go through crises like the one we have been through in the last decade.
mr president, it is now 11 years since the financial crisis began, and the great banking reform that was announced has failed. europe is no longer protected against a future financial crisis. the banking union is pushing for an ever-increasing concentration of the sector, where small and medium-sized banks are being devoured by the big ones. this situation of progressive oligopoly is difficult because it does not guarantee that no bank will be saved with public money. the european central bank is acting like the most ruthless of private banks, pressuring the banks to get rid of their low-quality assets, leaving their customers in the hands of vulture funds. consumer protection and access to housing are the last concerns of the supervisory body. gentlemen, we need a stable financial system under democratic and popular control. unfortunately, the banking union is clearly taking us in the opposite direction. we're not better prepared. we keep defending the bank against the people.

madam president, commissioner, the trade agreement signed in 2013 by the european union with colombia and peru has been provisionally applied for the past five years and, after analysing its implementation and relations between the three parties, we can say that it has been a win-win agreement. this agreement goes beyond strictly commercial aspects, since it involves a relationship based on rules, common values and international standards which has had a very positive impact on the socioeconomic development of the parties. it is also a tool to consolidate our strategic partnership with latin america, which is of vital importance to the european union. the trade agreement has contributed to economic stability, modernization and diversification of exports in colombia and peru. it is important for these countries to have a reference market outside latin america which will enable them to diversify their exports. the agreement has helped colombia and peru to modernise and diversify their exports and has benefited their small and medium-sized enterprises. the agreement has also improved access to these markets for european companies, not only by eliminating tariffs but also by reducing bilateral trade barriers. however, i believe that effective action must be taken by the commission and the member states to enable our smes to exploit the full potential of trade agreements such as this. we should welcome the progress made in finding solutions to the existing trade barriers, especially in the areas of sanitation and phytosanitary matters, but there is still work to be done by colombia and peru to resolve issues such as the certification of certain meat and dairy products, the protection of geographical indications of the union or the taxation applied to the importation of spirits. the agreement also provided for cooperation mechanisms between the commission and the governments of colombia and peru, particularly on trade and sustainable development issues. the aim must be to work to ensure that international labour and environmental law is properly applied. the agreement, which is accompanied by a roadmap, has also served as a follow-up on social and environmental issues. we can say that positive progress has been made by colombia and peru, but there is still a long way to go and we must insist on compliance with the provisions reflected in guaranteeing freedom of association, the right to collective bargaining, labour inspections, informal work, child labour or environmental issues. i would like to congratulate the government of colombia on the agreement for a bilateral and definitive ceasefire and cessation of hostilities with the farc guerrillas, and also on its accession to the oecd on 30 may, which recognises the important reforms undertaken in the country. i also encourage peru to advance its reforms under the oecd country programme. finally, i would like to remind you that this agreement should also have been signed with all the andean countries, including bolivia and ecuador, which for political reasons did not want to negotiate it. i welcome the fact that ecuador applied to join in 2015 as it realised the benefits it represented for its economy and that this parliament ratified its accession in december 2017. we must encourage these friendly countries to continue working in the right direction. there is still room for improvement, but they must be congratulated on the progress made and assured of the support of the european union.

mr president, commissioner, the european globalisation adjustment fund has proved its effectiveness since its inception in supporting workers made redundant as a result of globalisation. we were able to adapt it to include the economic crisis, as a consequence of their intervention, and now we have done it again to include automation and digitization. technological developments bring about continuous changes in production processes, and it is our duty to keep up to date so that the policies we propose are in line with reality. the union must continue to invest in people and promote the improvement of their skills, particularly if we are talking about a large number of workers being made redundant. i therefore consider it important that this fund should remain reactive and i also support, like my colleagues, the reduction of the threshold for redundancies in order to make the fund operational. in this way it is better adapted to the reality of european industrial networks, where mass redundancies are becoming less frequent, and it allows entry into small-scale labour markets.

president-in-office of the council. – mr president, the topic of our debate today touches on the very core of our union and what it stands for. the authoritarian and totalitarian regimes across europe in the last century remain a dark chapter in our continent’s history. our union is based on the common values and the general principles of respect for human dignity, freedom, democracy, equality, the rule of law and respect for human rights. its aim is to uphold and promote these values, which, as we are all well aware, have been increasingly challenged in recent years. fortunately, younger generations have not suffered under totalitarian regimes, yet there is now a risk that we are taking these common values and principles for granted. our common values have enabled the longest period of peace in europe. they remain a cornerstone of our democratic societies and they need to be safeguarded and constantly nurtured. today we face a number of challenges that put our open societies at risk, be it through xenophobia, divisive nationalism, discrimination, disinformation or violent radicalisation, to name just a few. if we are fully to understand the present, an awareness and understanding of the past is crucial. a lack of knowledge about the origins of the union and about the way in which it works increases the risk of discrimination. it also prevents citizens from developing informed opinions on the actions that the union takes. on the other hand, knowledge about the diversity, heritage and traditions within the union and its member states promotes mutual respect, understanding and cooperation, which in turn can strengthen a common sense of belonging. we know that education can play a crucial role in promoting our common values and in promoting a better understanding of the union and of each other. we are also all well aware that the union’s competence in the field of education is limited and that member states remain fully responsible for their education systems and for the design of their curricula. however, at a time when europe is looking to the future and seeking to re-engage its citizens, especially young people, around an agenda of shared values, we believe it is important to create a sense of belonging among europeans. in this spirit, the member states have therefore made a number of commitments, as evidenced in various political statements, be they council conclusions or recommendations, which provide a strong basis for cooperation in this area. at the gothenburg summit in november 2017, the eu heads of state and government chose education and culture as the first subject to be addressed under the new leaders’ agenda, underlining their resolution to do more in these areas. the gothenburg discussions were followed by the conclusions of the european council of december 2017, which highlighted how education and cultures are key to building inclusive and cohesive societies. in may 2018, the council adopted a recommendation on promoting common values, inclusive education and the european dimension of teaching. this recommendation was a follow-up to the paris declaration of 2015, in which education ministers stressed the importance of the role that education can play in this respect. the commitments of the paris declaration are as relevant today as they were then. in addition to our efforts in this area at national level, we need to make the best use of the union’s instruments and programmes, such as erasmus+, horizon, creative europe, europe for citizens and the european solidarity corps, the support initiatives that serve to promote our common values. we need to provide our young people with the skills and competencies to become active, informed and responsible citizens. media literacy and critical thinking are crucial skills in today’s society. our young people need to develop the critical analysis and understanding needed to cope with the ever—growing volume of information. they need to be aware of the need to identify correctly, and use, reliable sources of information and of the risk of disinformation. finally, it is of the utmost importance to promote and encourage tolerance, mutual understanding and intercultural dialogue in order to secure a better future. the role of educational staff and their continuing professional development plays a key role in this respect. it is important to learn how to address difficult or sensitive topics or controversial issues and not to leave them unaddressed. teachers need support in their new role in an ever more diverse classroom. this subject is closely tied in with the priorities of our presidency. as our prime minister outlined yesterday, one of our main pillars is the europe of common values. we aim to stimulate the solidarity and cohesion of the european union by promoting policies on combating discrimination, ensuring equal chances and equal treatment, and by increasing the involvement of citizens, particularly young people, in the european debate. to conclude, i can assure you that this issue will remain high on the council’s political agenda. thank you for your attention.
member of the commission. – mr president, thank you very much for having put this important and very timely debate on the agenda. learning about our history and analysing the complex forces at play between and within our societies is the basis for understanding the world we are living in today. knowing about our past is also critical for building the future of our continent and our countries. let us not forget that the original underlying idea of the european integration project – ensuring that its dark history does not repeat itself and preserving our freedoms, shared values and ways of life – needs to be defended every day. commemorating and teaching that past, as well as cultivating the memory of troubled times, are key to shaping a common future. it is important to include all totalitarian regimes – be they fascist, communist or others – as we do on the europe-wide day of remembrance for the victims of these regimes, on 23 august each year. the commission supports remembrance, research and education in the field of totalitarianism in a variety of ways. preserving the memory of europe’s totalitarian past is one of the core themes of the current europe for citizens programme, which supports activities that encourage reflection on european cultural diversity and on common values. funds are available for initiatives that reflect on the causes behind the rise of totalitarian regimes in europe’s modern history and commemorate the victims of their crimes. furthermore, europe for citizens is the union’s main tool to support initiatives that raise awareness of and educate about the holocaust. each year the commission invests eur 3.5 million in these projects. several operational grants support holocaust memorials and education sites. remembering the holocaust needs to remain a priority. in that context, the eu has recently acquired permanent international partner status with the international holocaust remembrance alliance. the commission is also supporting the largest-ever eu-funded research initiative on the holocaust, with eur 8 million, through the horizon 2020 project. it is called european holocaust research infrastructure. further, in the field of research, in 2015 and 2017 the commission published calls under the horizon 2020 programme to support research on cultural opposition in the former socialist countries and on improving mutual understanding among europeans by working through troubled past. take, for example, the project courage which stands for - cultural opposition – understanding the cultural heritage of dissent in the former socialist countries. this project has created the first digital database highlighting various forms of cultural opposition in former socialist countries. the project concluded that education and research on cultural heritage are crucial to support open pluralistic democracies. in the field of education, the union supports and complements national policies aimed at better understanding our history and shared values. the current erasmus+ programme has so far supported some 30 projects dealing with history and totalitarianism in the eu. these projects gave pupils and students the chance to learn about the past in a direct way and make changes in their own lives as a desired result. last year, the commission put forward a council recommendation on promoting common values, inclusive education and the european dimension of teaching. member states agreed on it after only several months; this was a real milestone. never before has the eu said so clearly how important it is to promote our common values, to create a sense of belonging, to teach about the functioning values and origins of the eu, and, most importantly, learn about the complex cultural and historical experiences in our member states. the commission strongly believes that education is also the most effective means of preventing antisemitism. this is why the commission is co-funding a study entitled the holocaust in contemporary education, a joint initiative with unesco. finally, we can raise awareness and understanding through our cultural heritage, and i am proud that the european heritage label has been awarded to sites of historical significance. sites such as poland’s historic gdańsk shipyard or the sighet memorial in romania. let me reassure you that the commission will continue to promote remembrance of totalitarian regimes, whatever their ideological basis. understanding our past is crucial if we are to live together and to build a better future for our continent.

rapporteur. – mr president, i also address myself to the commissioner and the colleagues who played the role of shadows for the annual report on the situation of fundamental rights in the eu in 2017. this report had to be relatively brief, which it is. when you consider all fundamental rights in the whole of europe during one year, it is clear that you are tempted to speak about a tremendous amount of things. we have avoided this and have focused on six main topics. some of them necessarily extended, all of them of undeniable relevance and of major concern: the rule of law, migration, women’s rights, media freedom, freedom of expression and assembly, racism, xenophobia, discrimination, hate speech and other forms of intolerance, the role and mandate of the european union agency for fundamental rights (fra). we agreed from the very beginning on the criteria under which we had to work on it. our main political and moral criterion is the common view that we didn’t want to produce a completely neutral analysis of fundamental rights in europe, but our aim was to make a joint reflection on the values of the union, not just to defend them but also to suggest ways and steps to improve the charter. allow me a personal remark. no one thinks that the charter will be stronger and more vivid if we maintain article 51, which should be interpreted in a wider way to avoid that we have to advance at a good speed but with the handbrake on. i am convinced that we have produced a good report. i will highlight just a few aspects. first, as for the rule of law, we stress that the eu’s ineffectiveness in ending the breaches of the values referred to in article 2 is undermining both trust among the member states and the credibility of the european union. migration is still a major concern. in 2017, 650 000 first-time asylum seekers applied for international protection in the member states. more than 1 000 refugees have drowned in the mediterranean sea. humanitarian aid has been criminalised. states have not been able to undo the knot of the dublin regulation. women’s rights are clearly defended in the text, now when in some countries and among certain people they are attacked or dismissed. media freedom, freedom of expression and assembly that in the past counted among the fundamental rights for free men and women have now to be restored, even in places and countries where one would not expect them to be under threat. artists or social leaders are also the victims, now and then. racism, xenophobia, discrimination, hate speech and many forms of intolerance are reducing equality and freedom among human beings. we have tried to show that there are many forms of intolerance and discrimination, that our life can only be built up if it benefits from a rich soil of justice and a good atmosphere of freedom. as a final point, we mentioned the agency for fundamental rights, fra, based in vienna, which is doing an excellent job and has never before appeared in our annual reports. fra should be active, not only in giving support when asked to do so but it should also be proactive in discovering and denouncing cases where human rights are at stake or have been abolished. the fra needs a new mandate. our 21 pages are, in my opinion, a text which is at once simple, clear and forceful, thanks to the shadow colleagues and to the advisers who decisively contributed to this satisfactory result.

rapporteur. – mr president, i would like to thank my colleagues for their comments and for their support. with your report, we will send the message that the promotion and safeguarding of human dignity, freedom, democracy, equality, the rule of law and respect for human rights can make europe unique and a worthy political project. it is only by placing the wellbeing of the people at the core of the european union’s policies and decisions that europe will re-engage with its citizens. this is why, although the charter sets out the basic rights that must be respected, we must continue to denounce and address the breaches and violations of their provisions. it is our responsibility to protect the weakest and confront the powerful.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat fraud. madam president, commissioner, mr hoyer, i am speaking today on behalf of the committee on budgets to set out the points which we have considered important to highlight in the opinion we have drawn up on the report on the activities of the european investment bank. and, for lack of time, i shall concentrate on the most important issues that we have included in this opinion. first of all, the eib must continue to strengthen its investment capacity to fill the investment gap we have, both in the public and private sectors, and to maintain its countercyclical profile through these investments. investments which must have a clear objective of job creation, but also of quality employment, and which must be sustainable over time. and in this connection it is also important to stress that support for small and mediumsized enterprises must be further strengthened; communication and access to information on all the programmes available to the bank must be improved so that small and mediumsized enterprises can participate more effectively. it is also essential - and not only because of the existence of the european fund for strategic investments - that collaboration with national and regional banks and development institutions continue to develop in order to improve the impact of investments and to provide appropriate technical assistance to project promoters. and in this same vein, but speaking of investments abroad, greater and better coordination with the development banks is also essential in order to ensure consistency in the mandates and, above all, to be more efficient and to eliminate duplications. and on the other hand, i would also like to highlight the bank's efforts to achieve that target of 25% of climate-friendly investments. we must continue along this path and improve this objective in the next period. and finally, as every year - and this is the last of this mandate - i would like to ask the eib to continue its work, to continue its efforts to improve transparency and accountability, as well as the control of financial intermediaries to combat fraud, tax evasion and avoidance.

the rapporteur. madam president, commissioner, the other day a journalist asked me if i thought this regulation was necessary and my answer was very clear: yes, absolutely. we have discussed rights violations in the european union several times during this term of office and we have also seen how slow and ineffective the existing instruments are. the european union is a community based on common values which we must defend and respect as citizens and as member states of the union. this is not a europe of rights and not of duties. when a country wants to join the union, it has to meet a number of requirements in economic, political, fiscal and judicial matters. these requirements are many and very strict, and that is why it takes candidate countries years to get in - if they get in. and once inside, what happens? once we pass that test, can we do whatever we want? obviously not. this review must be continuous and if deficiencies are found, they must be corrected and if not, an effective and proportionate system of sanctions must be established. i must confess that i would have preferred direct sanctions, but i understand that the treaty does not provide for them in these cases. so i think the commission has made a very clever proposal, using the tools at its disposal, in this case the european budget. but as i said in the committee on budgets, i think the european commission has also missed a golden opportunity, because if we put together the two ideas i have just outlined - respect for the values of the european union, but also protection of the budget - we are short if we stick only to the rule of law. because the values we are talking about are the values enshrined in article 2 of the treaty on european union: respect for human dignity, freedom, democracy, equality, human rights, solidarity, justice, tolerance... all those are in article 2. they are the ones who define our union and they are the ones we have to protect. but we also have to protect the european budget, and there is no greater attack on public accounts, solidarity and european values than tax evasion, fraud and unfair competition. and that is why it seemed to me essential that this should also be one of the values, one of the criteria to be monitored, examined and, if necessary, sanctioned. we cannot talk about equality, justice, solidarity if we look the other way in the face of fiscal injustice. in our meetings to prepare parliament's position, in addition to discussing - as you well know - the subject of the regulation at length, we also discussed and negotiated three main aspects. one: the protection of the final beneficiaries. when we are setting penalties through the european budget, we have to be very scrupulous about the mechanisms and make sure that those penalties go directly to the offenders and not to the final beneficiaries. and so i think that with the changes made - thanks to the commission's technical services we have been able to work on this - the safety net we have defined is much more guaranteed for the final beneficiaries. the second aspect we have also worked on is the panel of experts, because decision-making under this regulation is going to be a very sensitive subject. the european commission must have all the information at its disposal to be able to take a reasoned, objective decision, and above all, free from any partisan temptation, and this is the purpose of setting up a panel of experts: to advise the european commission in this task. and finally, the role of the european parliament. in the commission's proposal, our role was that of mere observer and this is not acceptable, because we are talking about values, but about the budget, and in the budget this house is also the budgetary authority, as is the council, and therefore we must have a say and a vote. i would like to end, madam president, with a phrase which the president of the government, mr pedro sánchez, said this morning during the debate: it is time to defend and protect the values which make our project unique.
i would like to thank mrs gardiazabal and especially mr sarvamaa for the work they have done in the committee on budgetary control, which has been very difficult and complex. i would also have preferred direct and political sanctions in the council, rather than having the commission and parliament carry out work which finally affects the good name of european financing: it is no longer very good, because it is what we lacked. but i think mr sarvamaa and mrs gardiazabal have got a good text where the part of the funds that is well protected is mentioned. because it is clear that without an independent judiciary, without independent judges, it is obviously impossible to protect the financial interests of european funds which affect the beneficiaries, the citizens. i think they have achieved that squaring of the circle, that is, amending or trying to change the habits of governments by means of financial punishment, but without reaching the beneficiaries. as for the committee of experts, i must say that i did not like it very much. i understand that, i understand why it has been done, but i think that taking decisions out of the hands of the political decision-makers, in this case parliament, which already reports on human rights within the union, always seems to me to be risky and ends up in a confrontation. but i understand why it was done and i hope we'll follow it very closely. in short, i think that a good text has been achieved, which is difficult and complex, but if we manage to apply it well and explain it, above all, well, we will achieve what we have been saying this morning: that in order to achieve the europe that mr macron is proposing, we must first of all protect it from those who want to erode it. and in this case, this text, i think it will serve that purpose.
