member of the commission. – mr president, this is obviously a very important debate that we’re about to have. in our democracies political debate can sometimes be fierce – even very fierce – but resorting to violence or inciting hatred is never acceptable. politically motivated murders, physical or other acts of hatred are shocking and directly contrary to our very core european values. earlier on today, this house already paid tribute – and let me join that tribute – to a fighter for freedom and democracy, the mayor of gdańsk, mr paweł adamowicz. for 20 years, he stood for those values. he dedicated his life to the service of his city and wider society. while i’m speaking about this subject, i cannot but also recall the death of a member of the uk parliament, jo cox, who was a passionate defender of the rights of everyone in society, including new arrivals from abroad, and indeed of the european union. we need to recognise that that sometimes individuals can be drawn to acts of violence – radicalised, if you like – by conspiracy theories, polarised debates and more radical ideology. there can be no free and fair elections across europe if there is a climate of hatred and threats of violence against candidates and those holding democratically elected mandates. unfortunately, we’ve seen that even members of this parliament are not immune from violence and abuse because of the views that they express, and we must deplore that. earlier this year, commissioner jourová spoke at the inaugural meeting of the european cooperation network on elections. this network is a concrete step forward in implementing the commission’s election package from last autumn. the package recommended deeper cooperation within and between member states to jointly identify and counter threats to our democratic processes and protect the integrity of our elections. we’ve had several exchanges over the last year on threats to electoral processes, including at an event in april, ‘democratic participation on electoral matters’, a conference in october on ‘election interference in the digital age’ and in november, the colloquium on fundamental rights. at all of these exchanges one message comes through: one way a climate of hatred and threats of violence can be created is through disinformation and smear campaigns, often spread through the social media or accelerated through the social media. there have been coordinated disinformation campaigns which aimed to discredit and delegitimise elections around europe, sometimes conducted by third countries and sometimes by private interests from within our countries that do not have citizens and our democratic processes at heart. responding to this effectively is a challenge. these threats don’t respect borders or jurisdictions. they do not fit neatly into how we’ve dealt with regulating elections and political speech in the past. a group can misuse personal data to target online disinformation or to attempt to intimidate voters through threats. other aspects, such as the often widely diverging rules on donations and contributions, and the opportunity that the online environment creates to get round existing electoral rules make it even more of a challenge to deal with this. that’s why we need to collaborate together to ensure that we can bring together the resources and expertise needed to strengthen our readiness to respond to and to resist and mitigate this kind of challenge. within the framework of the european election cooperation network, we are discussing what works, such as good ways to reach out to citizens to build their awareness and to retain their trust. and media literacy, an effort that has been pursued in sweden, before their last election was a good example. we consider new ways to involve citizens in securing the democratic process itself, as latvia recently demonstrated, by inviting citizens to give examples of political ads which were thought to break national rules directly to the regulators. and we discuss how best to make use of existing tools, from data protection to financial supervision, and how best to close gaps which may have opened up as new technologies and their use and abuse have come into this electoral space. we will look to see where we can deploy european institutions’ – our institutions – influence and competences to support and help the member states’ efforts. in particular, this means working to ensure that the internet platforms, the big social media platforms, live up to the commitments that they have signed up to as part of our various codes of conduct and good practice, the code of conduct on hate speech and the code of practice against disinformation. as you may have seen, we presented the first of what will be a series of monthly reports on the progress the social media platforms are making in tackling disinformation yesterday. on the subject of hate speech, we need to keep in mind that hate speech is not free speech. it should be an unwritten duty of all democratically elected representatives to condemn hatred and to refrain from incitement to it. in accordance with the jurisprudence of the european court of human rights, states may sanction, or even prevent, all forms of expression which spread, incite, promote or justify hatred based on intolerance. in today’s society, online hate speech poses a societal threat, which not only affects the safety of immediate victims, but has a more general chilling effect on the freedom of expression and debate, not just online but in our societies. our core objective should be to ensure that authors of illegal hate speech are effectively prosecuted. we must ensure that all member states implement the framework decision on racism and xenophobia. the challenges that european electoral processes face are too complex to be solved by any one authority, member state or even private-sector service provider acting alone. indeed, no one should be left to act alone in this space or indeed to hold all the cards and make all the judgments. rather, a comprehensive approach is essential to ensure electoral security and legitimacy, while preserving an open democratic debate, a level playing field and the security of all those involved in our democratic processes. we must never lose sight that all our efforts need to be fully rooted in protecting and promoting the rule of law and respect for fundamental rights, in particular the freedoms of expression and association, which after all is what we are fighting to defend in our democratic processes and elections. thank you for putting this on the agenda. we look forward very much to hearing today’s debate and following up with you subsequently between now and the european parliamentary and other forthcoming elections.

the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the debate we are having this afternoon concerns the regulation on the eu's anti-fraud programme, and it is a regulation which has two purposes. firstly, to protect the financial interests of the european union and, secondly, to promote cooperation and administrative assistance between member states, and between member states and the commission, in the field of customs enforcement and in the field of control and enforcement of agricultural rules. this programme is part of the continuity of the hercules iii programme and its financial amount has been adjusted - i hope the commission can be satisfied - to the framework of the current financial perspective. in this sense, the programme incorporates two fundamental systems. one system refers to the anti-fraud information mechanisms, which summarise the commission's enforcement in the customs field, and the other to the administrative complaint correction mechanism, through which the commission provides assistance to third countries. it is important to note that this regulation will enter into force on 1 january 2021 and will not imply an overlap with other european union programmes and, in particular, with other programmes in the field of the fight against fraud. i am referring to the olaf regulation, i am referring to the regulation establishing the european public prosecutor's office and i am also referring to the directive in the field of the fight against fraud. it is important to stress that the regulation determines the practical cases in which the 'scope of application' will be applied in order to avoid these duplications and, at the same time, that the co-financing margin will be a margin of 80%, except in duly justified cases where there are genuine financial interests of the european union that may be affected, in which case the margin may be increased up to 90%. i would like to say, mr president, that in addition to these two objectives, the report we are presenting and the draft regulation have three other specific objectives, namely to prevent and combat fraud, corruption and any other illegal activity affecting the financial interests of the european union, to support the reporting of irregularities, including fraud, in respect of the shared management funds and the pre-accession assistance funds of the european union budget, and to provide tools for the exchange of information and support for operational activities in the field of mutual administrative assistance. and, furthermore, with this programme, parliament considers that it would be very useful if those entities from countries which are linked to the union by association agreements could participate in this area of customs cooperation. we have introduced a number of aspects relating to the evaluation, monitoring and control of the anti-fraud programme. we have planned to include a description of the actions to be financed under this programme, an indication of the amount allocated, the maximum rate of co-financing of grants and, in some way, also the obligation to introduce, as already provided for in the draft regulation, a report drawn up for the european parliament and the council, and a final evaluation at the end of the three years. with these initiatives, mr president, we have sought to respond in some way to some of the concerns raised by the court of auditors in this area. i should like to conclude by thanking the rapporteur and the staff of the house for their work on this report.
i would also like to thank mr salafranca, with whom we have worked very well, for his report and also for the fact that it has clarified some of the aspects which we consider to be fundamental from the point of view of budgetary control. because, while we understand the commission's request or proposal for greater flexibility, i would like to ask commissioner vella how the commission sees the current proposal, as put forward by mr salafranca, as creating problems for the future european public prosecutor's office. we believe that it is essential to have an annual performance report, even though the programme is small, because we believe that there should be no overlap in the actions of such a programme, that there should be no conflict of interest and that they should certainly serve to complement and reinforce other programmes of the same type to combat fraud. and finally, we are also in favour of doubling the budget for the programme, but we need you to explain to us why you think, mr vella, that there may be problems with the european public prosecutor's office.
member of the commission. – mr president, i would like to thank the honourable members for sharing their views on this important topic. they are clear evidence of the continued support of the parliament for the fight against fraud and the protection of the eu’s financial interests. with regard to overlaps with other eu programmes, this programme is the only one specifically supporting the fight against fraud to the eu budget and, as such, does not overlap with the scope of any other programmes such as in the areas of justice and home affairs and customs. in addition, the periodical preparation of the work programmes, through appropriate inter—service consultations, will provide ample opportunity to explore synergies and detect possible overlaps. furthermore, the anti-fraud programme pursues a different objective from the customs control equipment instrument. the anti-fraud programme specifically aims at the protection of the eu financial interests and therefore covers not only the revenue side, but also the expenditure side through a range of activities, of which financing the acquisition of equipment is only one aspect. the commission will ensure that there is no duplication between the programmes during the implementation phase, in particular when establishing the work programmes, which will be done in close consultation with the other commission services concerned. as regards co—financing rates, the financial regulation no longer requires that co—financing rates are defined in the basic acts. therefore, the proposal does not fix such rates, in order to provide the programme with the maximum flexibility. this is a horizontal issue across proposals. all your remarks and the amendments that you decide to put forward in the vote tomorrow will be carefully considered for discussion during the next phase of the procedure. some of them touch cross-cutting issues common to all proposals for spending programmes and will be part of the general negotiations for the next mff. the commission remains fully committed to ensuring that the eu anti-fraud strategy is supported by a modern and flexible financial instrument capable of facing, promptly and effectively, the challenges of future years. in this vein, we look forward to supporting the negotiations between parliament and the council with a constructive and cooperative spirit.

on behalf of the alde group. mr president, the success of the multiannual plans for fisheries in the union is based on the seriousness of the scientific data supporting the decisions taken and the consistency with which they are applied to fishing areas and species. and only then does the concept of 'maximum sustainable performance' make sense. only in this way can fleets benefit from the stability offered by foreseeable quotas in the medium term. the commission has therefore decided to propose a new regulation on the protection of the environment. we insist on three points in order to eliminate them. first, better define the concept of 'best available scientific data'. we should only consider studies carried out with transparent working methods and a certificate of neutrality by sound technical authorities to be valid. secondly, to strengthen the guarantees for professionals against recreational catches of high-value species. the weight of recreational catches on stocks must be balanced and any competition between commercial and recreational catches on the market must be avoided. thirdly, to empower the european commission to act when national authorities do not exercise the responsibilities and powers conferred on them by this regulation under the regionalisation. adapting basic principles to specific situations should not be confused with not applying them. finally, we are pleased that the possibility has been removed that the council may suspend, even briefly and for exceptional reasons, catch bans imposed to restore a species. opening that possibility makes the saying "bread for today, hunger for tomorrow" come true. and in the case of fish stocks, 'hunger for tomorrow' means hunger for ever. and i would like to thank mr cadec and the other rapporteurs for the work they have done together.

member of the commission. – mr president, as mr ferreira mentioned, the eu and the ivory coast have a longstanding relationship in fisheries. the renewal of the protocol to the sustainable fishing partnership agreement will further strengthen this relationship. through this partnership, the ivory coast not only offers access to its waters to eu vessels, but it also processes the products stemming from these vessels’ fishing activities and further exports them to the eu. this partnership will also help improve the sustainability of the fisheries sector, in particular through fighting illegal, unreported and unregulated (iuu) fishing. combating iuu fishing is a priority for both the european union and the ivory coast as iuu fishing threatens the natural resources and lives of local fishermen depending on them. this will reinforce the ongoing collaboration with the west africa regional bodies and the european fisheries control agency on monitoring, control and surveillance operations funded by pescao regional development programmes. this new six—year protocol provides increased funds to support the ivory coast’s fisheries policy. it will contribute to the establishment of a meaningful surveillance capacity and improved governance, and it will also support the development of the blue economy, inland aquatic resources and artisanal fisheries. we have placed special emphasis on the benefits for local operators as abidjan is a major port in the region. indeed, the eu tuna fleet operating off the coast of western africa lands a great part of the catches in abidjan the rapporteur. mr president, during this term the committee on constitutional affairs has not stopped working on how to improve the current institutional regulatory framework, our rules of the game. that is why we have produced a large number of reports on the application of the rules governing our institutions. we are ripe for the final push on those issues which we have found particularly relevant. i have had the honour of being the rapporteur on the implementation of the treaty provisions relating to citizenship of the union at a crucial time like the one we are living in. 'collective public policies are the only thing that can create citizens with the trust of individuals', says timothy snyder in his latest book. the concept of citizenship of the union was introduced more than 20 years ago and today at least one generation of europeans has grown up as community citizens. and a generation of children needs adjustments and improvements in the concept of european citizenship so that they will soon be our young europeans. the treaties state that a citizen of the european union is a person who has the nationality of one of the member states. citizenship of the union is thus added to citizenship of the state. however, the law has fallen short of reality. about what young people and children already perceive. we have a responsibility today to accept the results that european barometers have repeatedly revealed to us. 87% of europeans are aware of their status as citizens - the highest percentage ever recorded. but there's a disconnect between what they perceive and what's real. there are shortcomings, there is a deficit and there is a need to give some of these freedoms a real scope. the citizens of the union do not exercise their right to vote inclusive, more prosperous, more responsible societies, with less risk of temptations to exclusionary populism. nationalist and populist ideologies promote exclusionary identities; once again we know on behalf of the s&d group. mr president, my group values and supports the ombudsman's role. as the vice-president of the commission has pointed out, it is a key institution in protecting citizens from instances of maladministration in the union's institutions. we therefore want this institution to continue to operate within the current institutional framework, but adapted to some of the issues that have arisen in recent years and on which parliament has spoken: for example, improving access to documents; for example, protecting or intervening in the protection of whistleblowers; and, for example, also taking into account the many cases of harassment of various kinds that occur in the institutions. but we do not want the ombudsman to be an actor before the court of justice of the european union. we want the sentences to be enforced. we want it to protect european citizens in this respect, but not to be a judicial actor. and we want it to have greater financial and administrative tools to do its job.

on behalf of the verts/ale group. – mr president, the reform of the ombudsman’s statute is a good opportunity to update its capacity. we want to include in the statute three competencies. first, on whistle-blowers, we want to make explicit that the ombudsman should be able to carry out investigations based on information by whistle-blowers, and we want to delete the references to professional secrecy in order to avoid any possible restrictions on future legislation on whistle—blowing polices. second, on sexual harassment, the ombudsman should be able to deal with complaints on sexual harassment without exhausting the internal procedures of the institutions. third, on public access to documents, we want to delete any restrictions on access to documents that narrow the scope of the regulation on public access to documents. this is how we will continue to defend good administration and transparency.

member of the commission. – madam president, i would like to thank the honourable members for the inspiring debate. as with most fundamental freedoms, there are also boundaries for the expression of free speech and for the right to assemble. when demonstrations turn violent and when there are instances of hate speech, it is for the authorities of member states to maintain law and order, subject to judicial review, and to ensure that the rights and freedoms of others are not endangered. in doing so, and while pursuing the legitimate need to uphold security for citizens and property, the authorities of the member states must ensure that freedom of assembly and freedom of expression are effectively respected and protected, in accordance with their national legislation and international obligations. the european union, through the fundamental rights agency and the agency for law enforcement training, supports the exchange of best practice and includes handbooks on respecting fundamental rights in police activities.
member of the commission. – madam president, i am happy tonight to address, at parliament’s request, the issue of large carnivores – iconic species of the european landscape. this debate is timely because, given the discussions taking place in many regions in europe, my colleague commissioner hogan and i have jointly addressed a letter to all the eu environment and agriculture ministers explaining the commission’s approach to this issue and highlighting the support we provide, and i am happy to do the same in this house tonight. having suffered a very serious decline in most areas of europe, large carnivore populations have been recovering in recent decades, and returning to countries and regions of their former range. they are protected species under the eu habitats directive and their recovery is a contribution towards nature protection in europe and towards halting global biodiversity loss. however, i am fully conscious of the challenge that the return of these species presents, especially in those areas where they had been absent for many decades and in rural areas with extensive livestock farming. that is why, for several years, the commission has been supporting the active involvement of all relevant parties in finding suitable and acceptable approaches to reconciling the conservation of large carnivores and the legitimate interests of the people concerned. this work includes supporting and co-chairing the eu large carnivore platform, bringing together key stakeholder groups to facilitate mutual understanding. through the implementation of a european parliament pilot project, the commission is also helping to establish regional platforms, to foster dialogue among stakeholders and local authorities, in the areas where conflicts generated by the return of large carnivores are more frequent, for example in romania, italy and spain. projects under the programme for environment and climate action (life) also contribute significantly to supporting the active involvement of all those concerned and a participatory approach, in order to find solutions based on coexistence. the commission is aware of the fact that, at local level, the wolf may be an additional challenge for farmers in an already difficult social and economic context. in those areas where traditional livestock-protection practices have been abandoned, the return of the wolf certainly entails additional challenges for sheep farmers. that is why the commission believes that the sector should be appropriately supported to reduce its vulnerability to predation and ensure its co-existence with wild carnivores. support is available under national and eu funds, through life and rural development projects, and further efforts are necessary to raise awareness among those concerned, so that all possibilities are fully availed of. in november last year, the commission amended the eu guidelines for state aid in the agriculture and forestry sectors and in rural areas, in order to allow for full compensation, up to 100%, for damage caused by protected animals, including veterinary costs or costs related to the search for missing animals, and for full reimbursement, up to 100%, of investments to prevent such damage – for example in electric fences or livestock-guarding dogs. regarding the calls from some quarters to address the challenges by changing our legislation, i would remind the house that, under its ‘smart regulation’ approach, the commission keeps the entire eu legislative acquis under regular review. in december 2016, the commission published the results of the fitness check evaluation of the eu birds and habitats directives – what we called the nature directives. this confirmed that the current legal framework is sound and remains relevant, including as regards the directives’ annexes. all the eu institutions, the member state governments and the record high number of citizens – more than 550 000 – who replied to a public consultation have supported such conclusions and confirmed that the birds and habitats directives remain highly relevant and are fit for purpose. therefore, the commission has been devoting all its efforts to helping member states and stakeholders to improve the directives’ implementation, addressing the weaknesses and challenges identified in the fitness check. to that end, in april 2017, we adopted an action plan for nature, people and the economy, to be implemented by the end of 2019. this action plan contains important elements related to the challenges of conserving large carnivores and addressing the associated conflicts. these include, firstly, the update of the guidance document on species protection under the habitats directive; and secondly, continuing and expanding support for the large carnivore platform at eu and also at regional level. thirdly, greater use of rural development measures will be promoted to support prevention of livestock predation by large carnivores. fourthly, there is the increased life funding for nature projects, including for the protection of species and for coexistence. fifthly, on-the-spot missions, ad hoc meetings and nature dialogues will be held to discuss problems and solutions with authorities and stakeholders. sixthly, a peer-to-peer support mechanism will help member states’ authorities to learn from each other in terms of implementation on the ground. the final element is the update of the prioritised action frameworks, which identify the financial needs related to species protection, including for damage prevention, mitigation and compensation, in view of the upcoming eu financial perspectives for the period 2021 to 2027. the updated guidance document i mentioned is a work in progress. it is being drafted in very close cooperation with member states and with stakeholders. after a first round of consultations, a second draft is currently being prepared and will be subject to a new round of consultations in the coming months. the updated guidance aims to deliver on the commitments in the nature action plan to ensure clarity and consistency in the interpretation of the habitats directive, taking into account the recent case law of the european court of justice. the commission will not propose any new rules or legal obligations. the guidance document will provide the commission’s view on interpretation of the species-protection provisions under the habitats directive. honourable members of the european parliament are of course welcome to share their views on the draft guidance with the commission. all these measures are aimed at helping national authorities and the relevant stakeholders. however, it is for the relevant national authorities to decide on the most appropriate measures in each case, in line with eu law.
on behalf of the ppe group madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the adoption and implementation of the habitats directive, among other measures, was intended to improve the sustainability of europe's natural ecosystems; animal species at risk of extinction could benefit from its measures. however, it has had a very harsh effect on one of the most important species in the rural ecosystem - livestock farmers and their families - with significant and constant economic losses. the wolf, the bear, the lynx have seen their populations improve. and now, for example, the wolf in spain even has a favorable conservation status in large territories. however, reality has shown that this directive is incompatible with traditional extensive grazing, which is precisely one of the activities in the rural world that we want and must protect. the damage to farmers is constant and the european directive has not been accompanied by sufficient budgetary measures to alleviate the enormous losses caused to cattle, sheep and goat farmers, and therefore these farmers are now the most vulnerable species. the farmer is in a clear decline, he has no way of coping with these policies which are causing him so much damage and which did not take sufficient account of the effects they would have on livestock farming in the european countryside, which is also still declining, abandoning an activity which is part of the cultural heritage of rural europe. the issue has reached such an extreme that even foodstuffs with a european designation of origin and geographical indication, which are directly dependent on extensive livestock farming for their raw material - milk - cannot take place. idiazabal, ibores or roncal are also species that will disappear if we do not have enough livestock. we must maintain the extensive cattle farms and we must do it with money, gentlemen.

because we recognise the serious social effects of the economic policies of austerity, especially in the southern countries; because we know that brexit forces us to think about a europe that is probably different as a result of the withdrawal of the united kingdom; because there have been major disagreements between the different countries, especially, for example, in the field of migration policies; because new problems, such as internal security and external security - the first of which is the problem of terrorist attacks, and the second of a very conflicted neighbourhood - force us to re-conceive european defence; madam president, according to a study recently published in the journal biological conservation, insects could disappear from the planet within a hundred years, and that would be a terrible thing. in fact, today, about a third of all insect species are threatened with extinction. the consequences of such a disappearance would be catastrophic both for ecosystems and for humanity itself. the authors of the study believe that the main cause of this species loss is clearly the use of pesticides associated with extensive agricultural practices. we must therefore change our agricultural model now by adopting a preventive approach, avoiding exposure to pesticides by adopting non-chemical and truly sustainable farming methods, such as crop rotation, physical and mechanical control or the management of natural predators. in the face of monsanto we must push forward the sustainable solutions that farmers want to put in place.

the rapporteur. mr president, i thank my colleague, david martin, and i also join him in thanking the ambassador of singapore, who has certainly been of great help to us all in the preparation of these reports, presenting us with a transparent and always well-informed picture of the realities of singapore. fifteen years have passed since the council authorized the commission to negotiate an agreement with singapore, and it was time to conclude this procedure. tomorrow we will take a step forward by voting our consent to the framework agreement on partnership and cooperation and to the free trade and investment protection agreements. today, once again, we send a strong message about the european union's commitment to international cooperation and multilateralism, against others - we know who. in a world where international cooperation is being called into question, the european union stands firm and stresses the importance of international cooperation. this agreement with singapore seeks to institutionalise relations which date back several decades and are based on a long history of friendship and close historical, political and economic links. the new legal framework for bilateral relations will provide a strengthening of cooperation between singapore and the european union. the aim is to cooperate on issues such as justice, security, climate change, development - issues that our citizens are very attentive to. i remember the geostrategic importance of singapore. it is an essential player in ensuring stability and regional balance in the asia-pacific region. and the security and stability of the region is important for europe, for european businesses and for europeans. singapore is the gateway to the asian market and a platform for european companies, strategically located between the major economies of china, india and japan. these agreements improve the investment climate and will offer greater certainty to european investors. i would like to stress that, within the framework of this partnership and cooperation agreement, we are going to set up a permanent joint committee, a committee made up of high-level representatives from both sides whose task it will be to work on a daily basis towards the achievement of the established cooperation objectives. we will be privileged partners in decision-making on issues such as international security, scientific and technological cooperation, in sectors such as energy, the environment, natural resources and transport, in particular maritime and air transport. we will cooperate on information society issues and, above all, on cybersecurity. it is important to cooperate on these issues, because it is a global field that knows no borders, and because our companies lose millions in cyber attacks, and together we can anticipate attacks and coordinate that fight. we will also significantly increase existing cultural exchanges, as well as education programmes for young europeans, such as erasmus mundus, and support new business and employment opportunities for our young people. singapore can become that platform for our young people into the asian labour market. i would also like to stress the importance of this agreement for global security and the fight against terrorism. the only way to combat this scourge that threatens our welfare model is to build bridges of cooperation with other countries, to exchange data and information, to stop funding and thus to make terrorist attacks impossible wherever they occur. this agreement means an open window for all european entrepreneurs and companies to establish business relations not only with singapore but also with other asian countries. more than 10 000 companies and entrepreneurs from the european union are based in singapore and use it as a hub to serve the entire pacific region. a stable legal framework is the cornerstone of any partnership agreement. by giving european entrepreneurs and companies legal certainty in their relations with singapore, we are opening up new business opportunities, we are promoting their investments, their growth and expansion. every time our citizens can develop their business ideas and projects freely and safely, we are creating the right environment to boost new jobs. i have already mentioned issues such as climate change, and i want to emphasize this. singapore's geopolitical importance in responding to natural and humanitarian disasters in southeast asia is crucial. the european union will now have a privileged platform to cooperate and participate in the decision-making process of the climate change policies adopted by singapore, contributing our know-how in combating climate change, a key policy of our union. finally, i would like to thank all the other rapporteurs for their help and cooperation in this report, and i am confident that we will be able to approve this framework agreement on partnership and cooperation with singapore by a large majority tomorrow. i believe that this is a great achievement for all of us and, of course, a source of stability, employment and a guarantee for the future, also for our international relations.

on the free trade agreement that we had in the committee on international trade (inta) last month reflects this excellent cooperation. i also want to thank the ambassador of singapore and his government for their cooperation and patience. i strongly support both the free trade agreement and the investment protection agreement. this is a win—win fair deal for both sides and for both consumers and companies. negotiations between the eu and singapore were launched in december 2009. nearly 10 years later, here we are, finally. singapore is by far the eu’s largest partner in asia, accounting for almost a third of eu—asian trade in goods and services. more than 10 000 european companies have their regional offices in singapore and they operate in a reliable business and regulatory environment. singapore is also a trade and transport hub to asia and a gateway to the major growth economies of the world. this agreement can be a model for other asian countries as it is the first in this region. with regard to the investment protection agreement (ipa), it replaces 13 old bilateral investment treaties between individual member states and singapore. tomorrow, i hope we will vote in favour of a new and modern investment court system. the ipa protects the parties’ right to regulate and to achieve legitimate policy objectives in areas such as public health, safety and the environment. moreover, there is no protection of investors’ profit expectation. furthermore, the investment protection agreement defines fair and equitable treatment, preventing forum shopping and parallel claims, among other things. lastly, i want to recognise commissioner malmström’s efforts to improve dialogue, accountability and transparency. growth in europe comes with trade and not with more public debt. given brexit and trump, multilateralism today is welcome and we should keep going in this direction.

in writing. it is important to differentiate between recreational use and therapeutic use of cannabis. it is obvious that cannabis is not a panacea, but it does have therapeutic properties for the symptomatic treatment of some diseases. take chronic pain, which i think is often medically neglected. cannabis is used as an adjunct to painkillers and other drugs that do not alleviate pain on their own. on the other hand, we must not trivialize the risks of cannabis use. according to the who expert committee on drug dependence, its use can cause adverse effects such as dizziness and impaired motor and cognitive function. more pharmacological, preclinical, toxicological and testing research is needed to ensure the quality, safety and efficacy of the medical use of cannabis and its cannabinoids are monitored, as well as studies to identify the potential risks associated with their use. the legalization of therapeutic uses in medicine should also be studied.

first vice-president of the european commission. – madam president, also on behalf of jyrki i want to thank you and the members for offering us the possibility to present our reflection paper on the european union’s road to sustainability from now until 2030 and beyond. sustainable development starts and ends with people. it is about upholding our way of life and upgrading the well-being of our children and grandchildren. it’s about equality, a healthy natural environment and a thriving green and inclusive economy. our starting point in moving towards a sustainable european future has to be the 17 comprehensive and interdependent sustainable development goals the world agreed upon and committed to in the united nations in 2015. these goals offer the most comprehensive and universally accepted framework to guide our work for the years to come. our core challenge for the next decade is to find a way to develop economically, continuously improving our living standards and well-being for the benefit of all, without depleting our natural resources, destroying and poisoning our environment and spurring climate change. what we need is an economy that grows within the limits of our planet and delivers prosperity to the many, not the few. to achieve these goals and to get there requires some fundamental changes in our production and consumption patterns. there are certain key game changing policy areas we in the eu have already started to deliver on and need to continue to prioritise. we need to move from a linear to a circular economy. we need to put our food system onto a fully sustainable path. we need to future proof our energy, buildings and mobility. but we will only truly be successful if we make these changes in a socially fair manner, putting strong social policies in place and making sure we leave no one behind. that’s the only way you can get everyone behind this policy. to do all that we also need to gear the so-called horizontal enablers towards a green and inclusive economic transition. these include education, science, research, innovation and digitisation, as well as finance, taxation, pricing, so that sustainable products and services become the most affordable ones, including responsible business conduct and fair trade policies. good governance is key as the very foundations we build on are the rule of law, democracy and fundamental rights. this is of course a global issue, especially now when others are questioning their commitment. we need to continue to be the strongest advocate for sustainable development in a multi-polar world, in a world based on multilateralism. this is also in our own competitive interest. the eu is at the origin of many of the most innovative and comprehensive sustainability solutions. we are best placed to be a first mover, blaze a trail for the rest of the world and reap the social and economic benefits of the sustainable transition while helping to shape global standards. (applause)
vice-president of the commission. – madam president, we all know that there is no planet b, thus there is no plan b, and we have to take the sustainability challenge seriously. but the positive thing is that sustainability is anchored in the eu treaties. it’s part of our dna. delivering on the sustainable development goals (sdgs) is not just a necessity, it is also a huge opportunity. it is about modernising our societies, about new forms of doing business and consuming, about reaping the benefits of new technologies and innovation. it’s about our future competitiveness. we already see that it is possible. the past years have shown that gdp growth is compatible with the reduction of co2 emissions. it is not about lowering our living standards but about being smarter about our resources. of course this requires a significant amount of investment. here, the investment plan can play an important role in bringing the private sector on board. the action plan on sustainable finance will provide investors with comprehensive information on what is sustainable investment and create a new market for it. the circular economy is another area where we can create a new market. we have started to do so with plastic waste, other sectors should follow. to be successful, the transition needs to fulfil some conditions. first, we need to invest more in education and training to ensure equal opportunities and fairer societies. second, we need to invest more in research, development and innovation, and also digitalisation, in particular in artificial intelligence. this has a huge potential, for example, in health or agriculture and europe cannot lag behind in this field. third, the rule of law and respect for fundamental values. we have recently seen worrying signs of leaders calling the very foundation of our democracies into question. the reflection paper is also a call to the rest of the world not to get tempted by easy solutions that may solve symptoms in the short term but that do not address the causes of our problems. we will continue contributing solutions, together with the rest of the world, in multilateral forums and through development cooperation, the external investment plan, as well as through open and rules-based trade. i am convinced that good cooperation between the commission, member states and the honourable members of this house can provide and strengthen the leadership of europe in sustainability.

i am speaking on behalf of the gue/ngl group. madam president, with this reflection paper the european commission is trying to sell us a green motorcycle again, a deception. it explains that the european union - and i quote verbatim - is well placed to be a world leader in the transition to sustainability, or that it has been a pioneer in this field. but if we look at the proposal in more detail, we see that the european commission's first concern is economic growth, but understood as the benefits that transnational companies can derive from this economic reorientation. for example, 'let's talk about agriculture', the first thing the commission says is that it can create new economic value of more than eur 1.8 trillion by 2030 and, if anything, contribute to the recovery of natural resources; but at no time is there any question, for example, of the large-scale use of pesticides that was discussed this week in this house, or the fact that the common agricultural policy favours large farms more than local and organic farming. nor is there any question of insufficient energy targets. in fact, with the data that eurostat has recently pulled out of its hands, it doesn't seem so clear that we are going to reach the common target of 20% renewables by 2020. i don't know, man. as i said at the beginning, the commission is either selling us a green motorcycle or it is selling us smoke. but the truth is that the root of the problem is not being attacked - a voracious and unsustainable economic system. the solution is to put the ecological transition under the umbrella of the interests of people and the planet, and not the sacrosanct economic growth. you can't fight climate change without those responsible for it losing their privilege.
madam president, in the implementation of the sustainable development goals, there is still a lot to be done. the failure to achieve the objective of sustainable production and consumption or the sustainability of the oceans, seas and their resources is unacceptable. even in the energy sector, where we can proudly say that the european union has managed to decouple emissions and economic growth, we have to admit that emissions have risen again in 2017. you can't fool yourself. the only path to development is social and environmental sustainability. and meeting the sustainable development goals is a moral imperative. the preservation of the planet requires decisive action, without pause. this is urgently needed to avoid the worst consequences of climate change.
in writing. today, our economic system, the way we produce and consume, is leading us to a serious environmental crisis. social and environmental problems are interconnected and lead to injustices that always affect the most vulnerable. we socialists propose a profound economic, social and ecological change, framed in the united nations' 2030 sustainable development goals. we believe that this change must focus on five areas: empowering people as citizens in democracy, not just as consumers, from the local to the european level, and as members of trade unions and civil society organisations; changing and limiting capitalism to ensure that private economic activity considers social and environmental impact and contributes to a better distribution of wealth and income; achieving social justice with no one left behind; generating ecological and social progress; facilitating change in eu governance and working methods to achieve a sustainable and equitable europe, with a new governance framework for sustainable development, setting out a set of binding policy objectives that go beyond the strict fiscal objectives of the stability and growth pact.

the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, i begin by reiterating my recognition that a european proposal for a health technology evaluation agency is timely and would make more europe. it is true that the european rules on medicines developed since 1965 in the wake of the thalidomide disaster have made a major contribution to improving health standards in the european union and that we also believe that there are areas for improvement. the european medicines agency evaluates and approves medicines on the basis of efficacy and safety, without regard to quality in terms of effectiveness or added therapeutic value. you might even consider that someone like me might not be ethical, and that it might put a burden of sustainability on health systems. but the fact is that parliament, echoing the citizens, wants to guarantee access to medicines and health technology. high prices in the context of the crisis were the trigger for these difficulties in access, but there is also a mismatch between research and medical needs, and more quality is also needed. there is an incremental excess of research at the expense of genuine innovation, some studies put the figure at 85%. moreover, even the high prices of medicines do not go hand in hand with the high therapeutic value added in many cases. in the case of cancer drugs, which have seen their price increase by more than ten times, only 15% of them have shown an increase in 5-year survival. member states have been conducting this quality assessment as part of the pricing and reimbursement process. since 2003, the european commission, through eunethta, has funded collaboration between these to approximate criteria, methodology, improve and increase clinical evidence and establish the clinical value of health technology. in addition, advances in genetics, the latest medicines for ever smaller populations, advanced therapies or the technology itself require ever more demanding clinical evidence, and in any case sufficient to be able to make decisions about it. however, despite the positive view of the member states of this voluntary collaboration, they have not made use of it. the european parliament also considers it necessary to deepen this collaboration and move to a stable scenario, with a regulated procedure and public funding, which improves access to health technology for european citizens, contributes to the sustainability of health systems and increases the quality of research, also aligning this research with the needs of patients. the european commission has presented us with a proposal for hta, justifying it by the need to improve the functioning of the internal market and thus the predictability of industry. even if there may be distortion in the internal market, this cannot be the main objective of the proposal, since this distortion may also largely correspond to the conception of the medicinal product itself as a consumer good and governed by the laws of the market. however, this regulation is not necessarily opposed either - and it may be able to contribute to such an improvement in the competitiveness of industry by stimulating quality innovation and improving the efficiency of research. the position of parliament has been to give a response, in my view quite balanced, to all these challenges that i have raised and, above all, to seek the necessary confidence in the process, guaranteeing independence, transparency, objectivity, scientific quality and external validation of the whole procedure. this allows the member states to play a clear leading role and to exercise control through their national evaluation agencies. and ultimately, ensuring that, while the clinical evaluation may be global, the decision is ultimately local. member states will be able to carry out their own reassessments to adapt them to their national contexts, within the national competencies of the pricing and reimbursement system, which includes specific clinical criteria as well as social, ethical and economic criteria, removing doubts about possible negative effects on the sustainability of national health systems, as we have been shown. at the same time, it opens up new areas of collaboration in emerging sectors in health such as precision medicine or the divestment of obsolete technology. in short, as i said, it is a balanced, timely proposal that guarantees patients and national health systems. so, in my view, necessary. what is needed now is a constructive and dialogue-oriented approach on the part of the member states, to which this parliament has always been open. otherwise, it may block the discussion needed to improve access to health technology for patients in the european union. it is not good to adopt an obsessional, anti-competitive attitude, without dialogue or alternatives on the part of certain countries, which can only lead us to repeat previous experiences with other health dossiers that only end up with the result that the only ones who end up losing are the patients. this parliament has worked hard and fast to be able to close this dossier in this legislature and to send a very important message to the european citizens, who have been asking us for improvements in access to medicines, to health technology; who have health among their priorities, as the eurobarometer repeatedly demonstrates, and who will be evaluating us in the coming months at the ballot box. i therefore call for a constructive position on the part of the member states in order to be able to close this dossier and give the response that european citizenship is asking us to give.

vice-president of the commission. – madam president, once again let me congratulate the rapporteur for her work and her dedication, and also the shadow rapporteurs for their support in the negotiations. coming back to some of the points which were raised during the debate: we spent quite some time debating whether this regulation should be extended to all currencies of the eu, but the point is that only euro transactions are the same everywhere, on the basis of the single european payment area (sepa); and only euro transactions benefit from the efficient payment infrastructures and processes that are available to all banks in the eu directly or indirectly. in the case of the euro, we have already created the infrastructure, and what we can do, with the regulation, is basically to make sure that banks are passing on the efficiency of this infrastructure to the consumers. but we do not have it for all currencies in all cross-border situations. let me stress again that this legislative initiative is a good opportunity to remove fundamental inequality among eu citizens and to unify the single retail payments market. this is of tangible benefit to europeans in their daily lives, so let’s make it happen.

member of the commission. – mr president, this debate and this week’s vote are very important, as mr de castro has said, not alone for what they represent but for what they will deliver. what this debate and the vote represent is an acknowledgment that, for far too long, the farmer and other smaller operators in our food supply chain have been disadvantaged by their relative weakness; but, more importantly, what this debate and the vote will deliver is protection for these farmers and suppliers of agri-food products further downstream. many members of this house have been consistent and vocal in calling for greater protection for the position of farmers in the agri-food supply chain – and rightly so. without that influence, i have no doubt in saying, today might never have happened. i am pleased therefore that the commission – and, of course, a very good commissioner for agriculture – could finally, and for the first time, response positively with a legislative proposal to ban certain unfair trading practices. before reflecting briefly on the contents of the directive on which you are about to vote, i want to congratulate the rapporteurs for parliament and the austrian council presidency for their efforts in reaching these landmark achievements – particularly mr de castro, for parliament, and ms köstinger and the austrian team on behalf of the council. i would like to thank all the shadow rapporteurs and all the other committee people who have been involved: mr tarabella, on behalf of the committee on the internal market and consumer protection; ms mcavan on behalf of the committee on development; and ms pilar ayuso on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection. i would include, as well, the shadow rapporteurs, ms mcguinness and ms mcintyre, and maria heubuch, elsi katainen, matt carthy, marco zullo and jacques colombier. all of you have played a remarkable part in ensuring that we are discussing this milestone legislation here this evening. it’s worth recalling, as mr de castro has done, that only eight months passed between the adoption of the commission’s proposal in april and the conclusion of the political agreement in december, so it demonstrates very clearly that if there is the political will a lot can happen in almost all respects in this house. it will now be up to the member states to transpose the directive, and i want to assure you that the commission will follow this process carefully and closely and i trust that this house will do so as well. the final agreement is one that safeguards our initial objectives and our rationale behind the legislation, which is to protect the weak from possible abuses of buyer power by the strong. for the first time, rules will be introduced at a european level that target unfair trading practices and provide protection for all eu farmers, as well as most agri-food businesses, against practices that are contrary to good faith and fair dealing. the directive will introduce a minimum eu level of protection against unfair trading practices that occur in the food supply chain. that level will apply in all the member states – which will remain free to go further, subject to internal market rules. for the first time, there will be a ban on 16 unfair trading practices which are imposed unilaterally by one trading partner on another. other practices will be permitted only if they are subject to a clear and unambiguous upfront agreement between the parties involved. the agreement that we reached in december will apply to anyone involved in the food supply chain with a turnover of eur 350 million, with differentiated levels of protection provided below that threshold. it is important to see this directive as part of a wider initiative to strengthen the position of farmers in the food supply chain. indeed, the agricultural markets task force, under former minister for agriculture cees veerman, called for a better legal framework on producer cooperation, as well as improved market transparency. i am pleased to be able to tell the house, and to be able to report to you, that we have also achieved significant progress in these two areas through the omnibus regulation, in which parliament was instrumental, including with the involvement of mr de castro and mr dess, and through the development of our market observatories. as you are aware, the commission is working too on a proposal to extend our transparency initiative to cover the processing and retail sector end of the food supply chain and i expect to be in a position very shortly to announce more details of this initiative. together, these three policy adaptations will allow farmers to seize greater opportunities as they present themselves in a market-orientated environment, and to defend themselves against market failures. in conclusion, can i reiterate my appreciation to all the members of the house, to the rapporteurs in particular, and to the austrian presidency, which has shown very strong support for this initiative that will protect not only the interests but in some cases the very survival of our farmers, as mr tarabella has said. nobody in the food chain has anything to fear from this legislation if they are behaving fairly.

mr president, the murder of a woman yesterday in my country has changed the subject of my statement because women are standing up to the world as they did on 8 march, when millions of women took to the streets to remind us that our rights are non-negotiable, to defend them and to fight against inequality. we are the daughters, granddaughters, sisters, neighbors and friends of those who suffer gender-based violence. we live in a world of prejudice that discredits our word. we live on alert when we go home alone. we suffer from the labor cause because we're women, we get less pay and less recognition for our work. our bodies are political because they want to decide for them, for us. they want to make us invisible and silence our voice like they did the two women murdered last week. this is gender violence that some political parties want to deny. and the european parliament must continue to call for investment in the fight against gender-based violence.
mr president, let us look at the following examples: european central bank: one woman on the executive committee out of five men, and one woman on the general council out of twenty-nine men. european banking authority: all candidates for the presidency are men. the single resolution board: all the male candidates. the single supervisory mechanism shall be headed by a male member. three european supervisory authorities: also chaired by a man. it is clear that power structures are unequal and it is clear that there is a gender imbalance in banking and financial services, specifically in their executive positions, and it is also clear that one of the values of the european union is gender equality and the gender perspective as a value and a horizontal principle. equality means more democracy. equality means safeguarding human rights. that is why it is so important to break down stereotypes, which our colleague mr sośnierz has not understood. we must break stereotypes and educate against stereotypes, and then we will have a fairer society, a society which is also economically equal. mr president, commissioner, what has happened with these appointments to the union's economic institutions shows that we have not heard the call for equality that european women made on 8 march. it grows every year because we don't learn. when we celebrated the 20th anniversary of the euro, only men spoke. then i wished that in twenty years it would not happen the same, but we are going the wrong way. equality is fairer, it is more democratic, but it is also more cost-effective. we're cutting off talent, we're missing out on potentially great candidates. they exist, we have to think about them and propose them. it's smart, but it's also mandatory. that's why we have to block these appointments. last march 8th, i received an image on my phone that said it all. think of the professional career as an athletics track: in the men's street there are no obstacles; in the women's street there are washing machines, clothes dressing machines, children, children's school appointments, household chores... our hundred yards are never free, they're full of fences. that's the first problem we have to solve. we need laws, self-criticism and commitment...
