member of the commission. – mr president, i would like to thank the house for this important debate. today’s debate has shown again that, as the european commission, we can count on this parliament as a strong ally when it comes to defending the principle of solidarity in our energy policy. this has been a major strength in our cooperation over this entire mandate. it has been our longstanding objective that when it comes to our external energy relations, the european union should speak with one voice. with the legislation we have passed during this mandate – the igas decision, the security of gas supply directive, and the amended gas directive discussed today – we now have the tools in place to do just that. as regards the gas directive, members raised a number of important issues. i would like to respond to the most important points raised. mr langen raised the issue of whether this legislation is discrimination against nord stream 2. i have to say that the revised legislation concerns all gas pipelines to and from third countries, and nord stream 2 is only the latest example of such pipelines which all operate under different legal and regulatory regimes. the recent legal and public debate concerning nord stream 2 only underscores the value of providing legal clarity on this issue across the european union. project promoters, including those from nord stream 2, should welcome the legal certainty the amended legislation will create. mr krasnodębski and ms wiśniewska raised the issue of the exemptions that can be given to nord stream 2 and who will decide on such exemptions. i would have to say that nord stream 2, like all new pipelines, could apply for an exemption under article 36 of the gas directive. the conditions for such exemptions are clearly set out in the directive. the national authority with jurisdiction over an exemption decision will be the authority of the member state where the first interconnection point is located. in the case of nord stream 2 it will be germany, but the draft decision by the national authority must be notified to the commission, which takes a binding decision. it may grant, reject or impose changes for the exemption decision by the national authorities. finally, mr rosati raised the issue of what the criteria are for granting an exemption. if nord stream 2 files a request for an exemption with the national regulator, it will be subject to strict conditions. as i said before, the final decision as to whether to grant an exemption stays with the commission. the exemption conditions include the following criteria. first, the risk level is such that the investment will not take place without an exemption. so if the investment cannot take place without exemptions it will go that way. second, the new infrastructure must enhance competition in the gas market, and also it has to enhance security of supply. these will be the criteria that will be applied objectively by the commission when agreeing whether to grant an exemption. i would like to conclude by thanking you again for your excellent cooperation. the new rules ensure that european union law will be applied to pipelines bringing gas to europe and that everyone interested in selling gas to europe must respect european energy law. i think that we have all made a major step forward in the creation of a truly integrated internal gas market, which is based on solidarity and trust, with full involvement and oversight of the european commission. i trust that in your vote tomorrow you will maintain that spirit and adopt this very important piece of legislation with a broad majority, as has been shown in the debate this afternoon.

in writing. despite the approval of new rules for the internal market in natural gas, to avoid monopolies and separate production from distribution, nothing changes with regard to the construction of the new nord stream 2 gas pipeline, as germany will continue to negotiate the details of this controversial infrastructure that will double the dependence on russian natural gas and help discourage investments in renewables. the eu has only made up the directive to legitimize germany in its negotiations with nord stream 2, an investment led by the former soviet state company now gazprom, and headed by former german chancellor schroeder, to build 1 200km of new pipeline across the baltic that will allow up to 110 billion cubic metres of natural gas into the eu. the diversification and security of supply provided by renewable energy is thus still being underestimated, and although ambitious emission reduction targets are agreed, it seems that the plan is to switch from coal-fired generation to gas-fired generation, i.e. one fossil fuel for another, which in addition in the case of natural gas is itself a greenhouse gas up to 86 times more potent than co2.
the next item is the report by mr gabriel mato, on behalf of the committee on fisheries, on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on the european maritime and fisheries fund and repealing regulation (eu) no 508/2014 of the european parliament and of the council (com ((2018) 0390 c80270/2018 2018/0210 ((cod)) (a8-0176/2019).
the rapporteur. mr president, emff funding is a key element for sustainable fisheries and the conservation of marine biological resources, for food security through the supply of seafood, for the growth of a blue economy and for the sustainable development of healthy, safe and clean seas and oceans. i would like to emphasize the importance of the european maritime fisheries and aquaculture sector, which involves more than 85,000 vessels, employs more than 340,000 people and produces more than six million tonnes of high quality and nutritionally rich fish, as well as seafood from fisheries and aquaculture. the socioeconomic impact of this sector is enormous in many coastal regions that depend on it and have strong links with local culture and customs. however, there are many problems arising from the implementation of the common fisheries policy, such as the elimination of discards or achieving maximum sustainable yield, in addition to those resulting from brexit. it is therefore important to safeguard the budget necessary to deal with these problems and challenges affecting the maritime and fisheries sector, and to take account of the very small budgetary allocation of the european union to this policy. and brexit should not be used as an excuse to cut funding. i am therefore particularly pleased that parliament has asked for a 10% increase in the budget compared with the commission's proposal. throughout the process with the alternative rapporteurs, whose work i would like to publicly thank, we have worked hard to strike the right balance between the need to continue to support the fisheries and aquaculture and processing sectors, while preserving fisheries resources. all the commitments were finally adopted in the committee on fisheries, and i hope they will be maintained in the plenary. i would like to highlight a few of these commitments. we do not want the seas and their ecosystems to be degraded, but we do want men and women to be working and to have a decent wage and working conditions. we do not want fishing vessels to increase their capacity to catch fish, but we do want investments on board that increase the space of a fishing vessel to improve safety or the living and working conditions of the crew or the quality of the product. we do not want to replace engines to get more power, but we want to replace old, polluting engines with modern, green ones. we have agreed not to give public money to build new ships, but we would at least like to make it easier to access credit, insurance and financial instruments, especially for small businesses that lack the capital to make significant investments. we like to pay special attention to small-scale operators, to the artisans, and that is why we give them absolute priority. we do not want to support operators to simply comply with the law, but we want them to be granted public funding when the law creates unbearable costs for the operators. we do not want to give money to those who do not comply with the law, but we do not want to impose double sanctions and conditions that prevent them from applying for funding. we do not want to finance holidays for fishermen, but we want to compensate them for the loss of their income in the event of a temporary cessation of fishing. we do not want to give money to fishermen to stop fishing and use this money to buy another vessel, but we want to encourage fishermen to stop fishing where there is excess capacity. we do not want to give money to aquaculture and unsustainable processing, but it would be absurd not to give a boost to our sectors that provide high-quality fish and continue to import low-quality and unsustainable fish. finally, we do not want the outermost regions to receive operating aid without justification, but we want to help these regions, which are far away and have structural constraints, to use the money available and to adapt it to their real needs. i am glad that we have finally opted for flexibility and simplification of the current detailed and prescriptive eligibility rules, and that we have partly moved away from what some call 'brussels micro-management'.
member of the commission. – mr president, on behalf of my colleague, commissioner karmenu vella, i would like to warmly thank the rapporteur, mr gabriel mato, the shadow rapporteurs and all the members involved in this important file for all their valuable work. the european maritime and fisheries fund should continue to support the objectives of the common fisheries policy and the implementation of the union’s maritime policy after 2020. therefore, the commission has proposed a budget of eur 6.140 billion in current prices for the next programing period, which will allow us to tackle the challenges ahead and achieve our ambitious objectives. support for the achievement of the objectives of the cfp remains a core priority. such support should ensure that fishing activities are environmentally, economically and socially sustainable in the long term while they can contribute to the availability of food supplies. hence the need for strong conditionalities for secession measures and leaving fleet renewal to private investment. however, support from the eu budget is necessary to help achieve and maintain sustainable fishing, based on the maximum sustainable yield and to reduce the impact of fisheries on our maritime environment. this includes support for innovation and investment in low impact, climate resilient and low carbon fishing practices and techniques. the emff is also a tool to support fisheries control and scientific knowledge. the commission has proposed to ring fence amounts for these areas of support to ensure that sufficient funding is dedicated to this cornerstone of fisheries management. i would also like to insist on the importance of giving preferential treatment to small-scale fisheries. in particular, under the commission’s proposal, small-scale fishers would benefit from a 100% rate of public aid. food security and nutrition are also of the utmost importance. fisheries and agriculture both contribute to this objective. an important challenge is therefore to encourage the consumption of fish protein produced in the union, which meets high-quality standards and is available for consumers at affordable prices. therefore, the emff can support agriculture, including fresh water agriculture and the processing and marketing of fishery and agricultural products. the emff may also support the development of the sustainable blue economy by creating conditions for the development of the sector, removing bottlenecks to facilitate investment and market development. lastly, the emff will support the union’s international action to promote and improve the international governance of the oceans. this is essential to guarantee healthy, safe, secure, clean and sustainable management and specially manage seas and oceans worldwide, in line with the 2030 agenda for sustainable development, in particular sustainable development goal 14. our proposal for the emff simplifies the delivery of the fund, compared with the rather complex architecture in the current period. this simplified architecture will not pre-define eligible measures at union level, but will give flexibility to member states in designing these measures. our proposal for a new emff represents an evolution rather than a revolution of the current regulation, with an important element of simplification.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat fraud. mr president, commissioner, we are talking about one of the regulations that is under the umbrella of the 2021-2027 multiannual financial framework and therefore also subject to the horizontal principles we adopt for negotiating long-term budgets. the european maritime, fisheries and aquaculture fund will be key to achieving much of the sustainable development goals. we are talking about food security, sustainable fisheries, protection of marine habitats and an economic activity that is fundamental to many of our regions. this economic activity must in turn ensure decent and quality jobs, ensure the training and access of young people to the fishing trade and support, recognise and make visible the work of the thousands of women who are linked to the fishing sector. and all of this can only be done with the right funding. we therefore not only reject the cut proposed by the european commission but also call for the amount to be increased to eur 6 867 million.

the rapporteur. mr president, i would first of all like to express my gratitude to all those who have helped us to finally reach agreement on the tripartite dialogue for this management plan for demersal in the western mediterranean. we are talking about the fourth management plan we are discussing for fisheries which are important in the european union environment and which is the first in the mediterranean. i would like to thank the alternative rapporteurs, all the technical staff and the staff of the fisheries secretariat for the work they have done, and of course the european commission, whose staff have also helped us a great deal to understand many parameters on many issues which are sometimes too technical and which were incomprehensible to us. i would like to thank you, of course, and also the romanian presidency, which has done an outstanding job during its presidency. and finally, we've got this deal. i sincerely believe that this agreement which we are bringing here today for debate and tomorrow for vote is the best possible agreement. is it the one that we would all and each of us particularly like? probably not, but if that were the case, it wouldn't be a deal. and, as it is an agreement of many parties and many interests, i think it is a great agreement. fish and shellfish stocks, the demersal species that are regulated and managed in mediterranean trawling, have been 'some more than others, it must be said' overexploited. this multiannual plan aims to reverse this trend and ensure that, in the long term, these species are managed in a more environmentally, socially and economically sustainable way. the plan concerns three countries - spain, france and italy - and a fleet of more than ten thousand vessels. some are arguing that it is a plan in which the sustainability goals have not all been achieved. others say it's too environmentally friendly. i think not: if some say we are on one side, and others on the other, in the end the middle point is the agreement. i would like to highlight a few points. for the first time, a multiannual plan on a mediterranean scale. it's an important fact. and i think it will serve for the next agreements and will set precedents for the same. we have adopted such important issues - which i like to highlight - as co-management for the first time in a management plan. member states may promote such participatory management at local level. the seals, an important and relevant issue also for protecting juvenile breeding areas and sensitive habitats up to a depth of 100 metres or six nautical miles from the coast when a shelf is too large, for three months a year, which will be for each country to decide. we have also determined that the maximum sustainable yield - which is a target we all have to meet, and which the cfp obliges us to achieve by 2020 - is not possible in this plan and therefore we will make every effort to achieve it by 2025. it has also been used to open up the limitation we had on the emff on permanent cessation. i would like to conclude my first speech by saying that, as this is an agreement and as a great effort is important, i ask everyone to give a great message with a great approval by a majority tomorrow.
member of the commission. – mr president, i would like to warmly thank the rapporteur, ms aguilera garcía, and all the shadow rapporteurs for their excellent work and all their efforts to conclude this important file in a successful and timely manner. the agreement reached between both co—legislators on 4 february is a historic achievement for the mediterranean. it is the first eu multiannual management plan in the region. based on the common fisheries policy, this plan provides a balance between environmental and socioeconomic aspects. it will introduce a limitation on fishing time per day and provide for a progressive reduction of up to 40% during the first five years. this should bring us closer to sustainable fishing by 2025, from which point in time fishing limits will have to fully respect maximum sustainable yield. for the first time, control measures for the fishing effort regime will fully apply as from next year, 2020. with this new plan, closure areas will also get an even more prominent role in the mediterranean sea. from the entry into force, we will have a three—month closure for all trawl vessels and more closures are to follow in the coming years. this will ensure protection of nursery and spawning grounds for demersal stocks such as hake. another step forward is the integration of recreational fisheries and co—management into the plan, the latter being very popular for managing fisheries at the local level in the mediterranean. when i look back to 2016, when we embarked on the path towards sustainable fisheries in the mediterranean with our medfish4ever declaration in catania, i realise the long road travelled to get the multiannual plan adopted and the tangible increase of ownership and awareness generated. i’m very grateful to see such great progress and that the final result, the multiannual plan, forms a comprehensive package of measures that will contribute to restoring demersal stock and ensuring that fishers have the necessary tools to address the transition towards better profitability, as in other sea basins. a new era in the western mediterranean sea will start with this plan, one in which concrete measures will be progressively implemented to reduce fishing mortality until we reach sustainable limits. i am confident that this new plan is the right way to go. it will ensure that fisheries have a prosperous future in this sea and that fishermen and fisherwomen will be the first ones to benefit from that. the plan serves as an important testimony of the possibility to progress in the mediterranean when there is a political will to do so. it should therefore pave the way for other ambitious plans to advance from both the side of the eu and multilaterally in the general fisheries commission for the mediterranean. during the trilogue, the commission committed to making three statements relating to the best available scientific advice, the inclusion of depth intervals as a criteria for the segmentation of the fishing effort, and regional cooperation. these statements are part of the final compromise and the commission will submit these statements for the minutes.
on behalf of the ppe group mr president, this agreement is presented by some as a decisive step towards sustainability in the mediterranean sea, where most fish stocks are apparently overexploited. but, once again, the pressure from various actors, the usual suspects, led to an agreement where the main and almost sole focus is environmental sustainability. i can only share the concerns of the fishermen that drastic cuts in fishing effort - a 40% reduction over the next five years - will have irreparable consequences. because in the last ten years, in my country, spain, the number of trawlers has already fallen from 900 to 600. i'm not sure other countries have made the same effort. but this isn't the worst part. the worst thing is that the proposed measures, and i am referring here mainly to the ban on trawling, have no scientific basis. they are arbitrary and rigid. direct bans are never constructive. they are simplistic, one-dimensional, disproportionate and unfair. a sudden and arbitrary provision of trawl fishing is a very bad precedent, which could lead to absurd restrictions in the future. the proof is that until now there was a prohibition on fishing within a fifty-meter isobara three miles from the coast. now the trawlers will have to leave the area where they have always fished and move further away for three months, a hundred metres from the isobara or six miles from the coast. this means in practice a total ban on trawling in most of the mediterranean, as this fleet operates mainly on the continental shelf, which mostly coincides with the proposed depth limit. in addition, the continental shelf ends abruptly in many areas, reaching a great depth of a few miles, making it impossible for trawlers to fish beyond that area. it goes without saying that bottom trawlers are the main suppliers of food to mediterranean ports, auctions and ancillary industries. so if trawlers have to stop fishing for three months every year, these sectors will also be deeply affected. crawling, like any other art, should not be demonized. we must avoid conflicts between different fishermen, between small and large-scale fishermen. all our fishermen contribute to the supply of nutritious fish and that is why our position will be to vote 'no' in the vote tomorrow.

the burning of the notre-dame cathedral in paris has again made us aware that we are bound by something more important and more profound than treaties. today we understand better the essence of that which is common, we know how much we can lose. and that we want to defend it – together. last week the european council of 27 leaders, in agreement with the government of the united kingdom, granted a flexible extension of the article 50 period until 31 october this year. this extension gives our british friends more time and political space to find a way out of the current situation. i hope that they will use this time in the best possible way. the european council will be awaiting a clear message from the uk on a way forward. if the withdrawal agreement were to be ratified, the extension period will automatically end on the first day of the following month, meaning that the uk would leave the union on that day. it is clear to everyone that there will be no re-opening of the withdrawal agreement. however, to facilitate the ratification process, the eu27 is ready to reconsider the political declaration on the future relationship, if the uk position were to evolve. last week, the european council changed the logic of granting a much shorter extension than requested by the uk, to giving an extension that is much longer. i proposed such a change, as in my view it has a few advantages. first and foremost, only a long extension ensures that all options remain on the table, such as ratification of the current withdrawal agreement, or extra time to rethink brexit, if that were the wish of the british people. second, this extension allows the eu to focus on other priorities that are at least as important, like trade with the united states or the new eu leadership. i know that some have expressed fear that the uk might want to disrupt the eu’s functioning during this time. but the eu27 didn’t give in to such fear and scaremongering. in fact, since the very beginning of the brexit process, the uk has been a constructive and responsible eu member state. and so we have no reason to believe that this should change. third, this flexible extension delays the possibility of a no-deal brexit by over six months. thanks to this, millions of people and businesses have gained at least some certainty in these unstable times. one of the consequences of our decision is that the uk will hold european elections next month. we should approach this seriously, as uk members of the european parliament will be there for several months, maybe longer. they will be full members of the parliament, with all their rights and obligations. i am speaking about this today because i have strongly opposed the idea that during this further extension, the uk should be treated as a second-category member state. no, it cannot. therefore, i also ask you to reject similar ideas, if they were to be voiced in this house. i know that on both sides of the channel, everyone, including myself, is exhausted with brexit, which is completely understandable. however, this is not an excuse to say: “let’s get it over with”, just because we are tired. we must continue to deal with brexit with an open mind and in a civilised manner. because whatever happens, we are bound by common fate, and we want to remain friends and close partners in the future. during the european council one of the leaders warned us not to be dreamers, and that we shouldn’t think that brexit could be reversed. i didn’t respond at the time, but today, in front of you, i would like to say: at this rather difficult moment in our history, we need the dreamers and dreams. we cannot give in to fatalism. at least i will not stop dreaming about a better and united europe. dear friends, this is our last meeting in your current term. i hope to have the opportunity to meet most of you after the elections. agenda. with that in mind, i want to be very brief. last week the european council, in an agreement with the united kingdom, took a united and responsible decision to grant an extension of the article 50 period until 31 october this year. this was an acceptable outcome for three main reasons. first of all, and with the support of this house, we have adopted the necessary contingency measures and we are ready for a no-deal brexit. the only ones who would benefit are those who resent multilateralism and seek to undermine the global legal order, and in any case we will never kick out one of our members. secondly, we have protected the integrity and the functioning of this house and all our institutions. if the united kingdom is a member on 23 may, it must hold european elections. if it does informed, in line with article 218 (10) tfeu, in relation to the work of the joint committee and the specialised committees established by the agreement on the withdrawal of the united kingdom of great britain and northern ireland from the european union and the european atomic energy community (the 'withdrawal agreement'). in order to enable the european parliament to exercise fully its institutional prerogatives throughout the process in accordance with the treaties, the commission will ensure that parliament receives sufficient and timely information before and after the meetings of the joint committee or the specialised committees of the withdrawal agreement. moreover, the commission considers that given the exceptional nature of the withdrawal agreement based on article 50 referred to in article 20 of the protocol on ireland/northern ireland that the protocol shall cease to apply in whole or in part. therefore, in relation to these decisions, the commission will inform the european parliament sufficiently in advance of its intention to submit a proposal for a decision on the position to be taken in the joint committee, and of the substance of its envisaged proposal. the commission will take utmost account of any comments of the european parliament in this respect. it commits, in case it does not follow ep position, to explain the reasons for which it did not. the commission understands that, in view of the short time frame available, the matter will be handled in the european parliament as a matter of urgency. the commission will then forward its proposal to the european parliament for information at the same time as it sends it to the council for adoption in accordance with article 218 (9) tfeu. the commission recalls that these practical arrangements must be seen in the context of the exceptional nature of an agreement based on article 50 teu and do not constitute a precedent for any other agreements.

the rapporteur. madam president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i have the honour to present here the work of a whole team, to whom i am grateful for the hard work they have put in over many months, but under pressure of time, to produce or propose the production of a directive which in some way builds on an earlier directive, which was adopted 28 years ago, and goes much further. i will begin by stressing the political importance of this directive at this time. this directive is part of the development of the social pillar which this parliament will always have the honour of having proclaimed in gothenburg last year. it is a first - i would say a giant - step towards the practical and concrete implementation of the rights contained in the social pillar and, in that sense, it is a directive which affects all workers in the european union and, therefore, all citizens who are generally either preparing for work or working - if they can - or enjoying the rights they acquired while working. it therefore affects five hundred million european citizens who are called to the polls within a month. that is why it is important that this directive be adopted in this parliament, which has been a balancing act between all the forces involved. this directive - let me be very clear - sets out the same minimum rights for all workers in europe: minimum rights. it does not lay down laws, it does not lay down methods, it does not lay down practical arrangements for their implementation, because that is what the member states will do. let me be very clear: there is no interference with the principle of subsidiarity; what it establishes are 'rights' and 'minimums' so that in europe we can speak of a social europe in which professional life can develop. i can only dwell on the content of the directive because it is what you know best and have read most: there are rights to information which have been greatly improved in comparison with the 1991 directive; there are rights to non-abuse, to non-abuse of probationary periods; and there are rights to training, which are absolutely universal in europe from now on or when it is transposed, but which are already a reference. and the great contribution of this text: substantive rights are given particularly aimed at all new forms of recruitment - on demand, platforms, what is called precarious work, whatever you want. all these workers, who are now in a kind of limbo that deprives them of their rights, will now have the reference of the court of justice of the european union and the reference of this directive so that no one can abuse or over-exploit the indispensable flexibility that is recognized. the directive also has its importance in the case of the level playing field - something that is not noticed or not so much said - that is, it ensures that the famous spectre of social dumping will never be at the expense of a minimum quality of life for workers, since this will be the same throughout europe. please bear in mind that we are building europe - which was destroyed yesterday in a regrettable way - and in particular social europe. thank you very much to all who have helped me in this work.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european union's labour market is not distorted by the introduction of new technologies, and that the european union is not forced to adopt new policies. this directive will also cover and protect platform workers, digital platform workers, who in many member states today have inefficient legislation to protect them socially. it includes relevant measures to combat abuses in zero-hour contracts or on-demand work. we must thank and acknowledge the work done by the european commission, and especially by our commissioner for employment and social affairs, mrs thyssen, by the european parliament and those of us who have been responsible for this dossier, and by the council presidency, the romanian presidency, which has been able to push through, in this last plenary session, a directive which shapes the european pillar of social rights. because it must be said that we are not just passing a regulation today. today we are showing a way, we are pointing a way for europe. a useful europe that protects, recovers and reclaims its social soul, that makes the european pillar of social rights a reality, not just a list of good intentions, and that wants it to be grounded in rules, tools and budget. why would you do that? because today the european social dimension is not the consequence of integration. today it is the precondition for european integration. we need to dampen and combat inequalities. we need to protect those who are displaced by globalisation and create economic security and job security. it is the only way to protect and nurture a fragile european democracy.
i am speaking on behalf of the gue/ngl group. madam president, i would like to thank the rapporteur for the work he has done and at the same time regret that the council has once again blocked any progress on the rights of european workers. the mandate of parliament ensured rights for workers in the most precarious conditions and the text we are about to vote on has left them with virtually no protection whatsoever. the emergency services, security forces, civil servants, seafarers, domestic workers under certain conditions and those with contracts of less than 12 hours per month, among many other workers, have been excluded. as the trade unions say, these exemptions are discriminatory and a dangerous precedent with respect to the european union's approach to minimum rights which by definition must be universal. the opportunity to build a social europe demanded by the workers has once again been lost. but what is being brought to the table is a much deeper problem, and that is the institutional framework of the european union, where the council - the member states - permanently blocks the decisions of the european parliament, which is the one the citizens vote for. you are the ones who are contributing to the widening of the public disaffection in the institutions and, with it, the advance of the extreme right. when they try to correct the course, they are already too late.
madam president, despite the good work of parliament - and i want to thank the people who have devoted themselves to this dossier - the council has watered down key elements of this piece of legislation which is fundamental for social europe. we have lost an inclusive and comprehensive definition of what a worker is, and the final text also offers great possibilities for member states to grant exemptions for all workers working less than 12 hours a month and also for a long list of professions, as the trade unions have denounced. in addition, a written contract is only required from the seventh day onwards, and in practice this means that for those who contract under the table, a worker will only have been there for six days when the labour inspector shows up. finally, as has been said, the shameful zero-hour contracts that many of our fellow citizens suffer from are not prohibited either. the reality is that a growing number of workers who are now working in precarious jobs are not sufficiently protected. the social europe deserves ambition and conviction, not the constant and exasperating debate to which we are accustomed in the council, despite the repeated requests of the european parliament.
madam president, new forms of work, such as on-demand work, based on extreme flexibility of regulation, instability and total availability, cannot continue to be, as they have been, new forms of cheap and precarious employment that feed on people who are left out of the system. this directive could have been ambitious and inclusive because its objective was to provide certainty for the labour market. however, by excluding from zero-hour contracts or from the chapter on minimum requirements groups such as the public emergency service, civil servants, researchers or seafarers - among others - it does not protect the people who need it most, many of them women, as is the case with domestic workers who perform domestic and care work and who, once again, have been left out of this legislation, something that is not understood, especially after this house passed a report to dignify their conditions. we cannot support this exclusionary and unfair regulation with those who need it most.
member of the commission. – madam president, i have already thanked the rapporteur, but let me also thank the shadow rapporteurs and also the romanian presidency for their constructive and successful negotiations. honourable members of parliament, with the proposed directive on transparent and predictable working conditions, we focus on what is really necessary for workers in today’s labour market. flexibility is today inevitable, just like digitalisation. therefore, we have not sought to prohibit new types of employment, but to support the workers concerned with protection against excessive practices and with the minimum of predictability that everybody needs to organise life. the implementation of this directive will be a common task for member states, employers and workers, with all the adequate room for social partners to make the rules a success on the ground. i call on you to support the directive. it’s a crucial measure of social justice and solidarity for all our citizens. as i said before, madam president, this directive is also a major achievement to make the european pillar of social rights a reality. we should all be proud of this milestone. honourable members, allow me to conclude by making the connection between this directive and our other initiatives – posting of workers, protection against cancelled work, access to social protection for all, the accessibility act, the skills agenda, a more european semester and, not to forget, work-life balance. i believe all these initiatives, those decisions, they show what this commission and this parliament, together with the council, have done during our mandate, bringing social europe back at the centre of the union’s action. the rapporteur. madam president, i have the utmost respect for those who are expressing reservations, and i will answer only those who are. if it is any consolation, which i do not think it is, i am also frustrated that we did not go further, but my job as a representative of parliament was to find a balance. basically, what you notice are three "pains", we might say. the first is that it does not cover everyone, because three hours a week and 12 hours are required. it is true, and we would have preferred it to encompass the whole world; but you notice, anyway, the advance with what we had before, which asked for two months. in any case, i would remind you that we have asked the commission to exercise a great deal of active vigilance so that, if contracts of, say, 11 hours a month proliferate, then obviously measures will have to be taken. secondly, there is also the issue of exclusion. i have not understood them, i do not approve of them, i do not understand these lobbies - for example the sea workers - but there was no way to reach a balanced agreement without going through them. i say that calmly. and then i find myself facing zero hours. we have made zero hours extremely difficult and, moreover, they are, from this moment on, unrepeatable. they can't be renewed. at this point, i would like to ask my colleagues to ask themselves the same question i have asked myself: is this a good thing, even if it is not perfect, is this a good thing for the future of european workers? is that much better than nothing? my conclusion has been that yes, and i ask you, respecting your ambitions, absolutely respecting your manhood of good or womanhood of good in criticizing the text, to consider whether the perfect is not the enemy of the good and whether it is not worth, in any case, a strong support of the whole of parliament to this stage in the construction of social europe.

problem exists, that it is not the quasi-invention of someone who has no other problems, and so on. we've heard a lot of it. the fact that we have a directive on the table today that recognizes that there is a problem, and it's the unfair commercial practices directive, i think that's a shift. where were we a year and a half ago? i had on my desk tests from eight member countries that were done using different methodologies. i've been in very tough negotiations with industry representatives, food and beverage industry representatives, brand association representatives, and i've heard arguments like, "well, these tests are used in different ways, apples, pears and so on, it's not comparable, it's not relevant, we're not going to look at it". so we've done a methodology, we've invested in it, we're now testing the second set of products that are being selected by the member countries, and we're finding that about 20 to 30 percent of the products have the significant differences that we're targeting with this directive. the methodology that we've developed also says how do they have inspections, whether it's food or trade -- we don't tell the states who to deal with that, so i'll call the inspections -- how do they have inspections to collect samples from different countries and compare them and subject those samples to testing. we're there today, we have the methodology ready and it can be said that it can be continued. to your arguments: almette, what else was there, chocolate, ice cream, well, those are the things that we are focusing on, that we are so concerned about, and where we should trust these inspections to take samples, put them to the test and say clearly that less cocoa in chocolate is a counterfeit food and cannot continue, that milk powder instead of cream is a counterfeit food that must disappear from the market and so on. these are the things that can be addressed under this directive, these are the things that people are bothered by. let's have a little more faith in those who do the market surveillance that they'll go after these cases case by case and be brave enough to apply this new directive. dr. rush spoke of vague legal terms, which is of course a risk with any legislation. imagine if we were to characterize it by denying different qualities, but you couldn't really work with quality as a concept. i would like to remind you that this is not a directive which only deals with foodstuffs, but also with products as such. by withdrawing that thing as consumer commissioner, i basically spread it to all products. by the way, we're starting to do a drug testing methodology now. so we're talking about cars, building materials, a whole range of other products. so we had to define, in some way, what unfair business practices are. so please, let's have faith in our inspections that they're going to go after these cases and they're going to fairly measure case by case and they're going to sanction these things. i'm also concerned about what's happening in my country. i know the secretary of agriculture wants to get to the bottom of this. market surveillance authorities are preparing to assist with the relevant national legislation so that this can be applied in practice. there's one other thing that we weren't aware of a year and a half ago. mr. whisperer here said to get more active citizens involved. that's exactly what can't be done now, because neither the citizens who are annoyed and who only have suspicions but no evidence, nor the chains and retailers know that the producer has different ingredients under the same brand. this directive requires them to report it, and if they allow themselves to do such a thing, that there's a different composition, they'll have to prove why. the counterfeiting of the product is not an objective and justifiable distinction. it's just not for me. and i trust that won't be the case for the inspections. so for me, who, as you know, proposed a stricter regulation, and i take this as a compromise, as the art of the possible, because as we heard, most member states were against, there are two ways. trying to help the implementation in the member states to work, to get counterfeit food off the market, is one thing, but that means fair and bold market surveillance. brave in the sense of going with the directive, not going after it, but being consistent. second, of course, the awareness of the public and retailers to look for where the information is, what information is relevant to what product. of course, the third thing the rapporteur. i am very pleased that after 20 years in this parliament my last speech is as rapporteur on the food chain, because i came here 20 years ago, as i said, in the midst of the mad cow crisis, after having been responsible for food and the agri-food industry in spain. i am actively involved in the regulation that gave rise to efsa and have been involved in all food legislation continuously over the years. today i can say with full knowledge of the facts that the european union has the strictest food legislation in the world and that we are a benchmark in food safety. i can say that our food industry is excellent, innovative and competitive, and i can say that efsa, for which i am the contact person for this parliament, has done a great job since its creation in accordance with the legislation in force. however, the regulation which created it in 2002 needed to be updated, not only because time has shown us where improvements could be made, but also because the citizens of the european union are increasingly interested in the food chain risk assessment process and in the transparency of the scientific studies on which decision-making is based. i only regret that this legislation has been rushed through, with little time to debate and under tremendous media pressure, which is not the best scenario. i think that calling this regulation the 'general food law' is a bit pretentious because it only addresses the issue of transparency. we cannot forget that in our food safety system, the responsibility for risk determination lies with the authority, but not risk management. i do not, however, wish to downplay the agreement we have reached; i sincerely believe that we have achieved our objective of ensuring a decision-making procedure, based on scientific evidence, which maintains a high level of public health and safety in the european union. at the same time, i think we can generate increased public trust in decision-making by making it more transparent. in order to ensure greater transparency, citizens will have immediate access to the scientific studies supporting the authorisation applications; that is, non-confidential information will be published at the moment when the application is considered valid or admissible. in this spirit of transparency, a database will be set up to ensure that companies submit all studies when they apply for authorisation and do not leave unsubmitted those that are unfavourable to them. in addition, companies that fail to comply with this obligation may be penalised. with this agreement we have also managed to strike a reasonable balance between transparency and the interests of industry in order to continue to encourage innovation in the food sector in the european union; that is to say, the disclosure of information will be without prejudice to industrial or intellectual property rights. in addition, to prevent such information from being used for unfair commercial purposes, certain safeguards have been introduced at the time of disclosure of the information, such as traceability. as regards the organization of efsa, i can only be pleased for two reasons: firstly, because parliament will now have two representatives on its board of directors, and secondly, because the participation of the member states in the technical and scientific committees will be increased. this will involve scientists from all member states more closely in the authorisation procedures. as regards the list of confidential items, it is important that the manufacturing or production process is included as a confidential item. it is also necessary to keep innovative ideas included in the confidential elements. finally, the positive part of this agreement, which is risk assessment, will continue to be based on scientific evidence, but at the same time it will improve transparency in decision-making. i am only sorry that the process has not been homologated with those of the european medicines agency or the european chemicals agency. and i'm calling for a vote in favor of this deal.

the rapporteur. madam president, mr vice-president of the commission thank you very much for your presence ladies and gentlemen, when we embarked on the adventure of this report it did not seem possible: i found myself faced with a territorial and political division that was unsalvageable. then, in the context of the tripartite dialogues between the commission, parliament and the council, after difficult negotiations we reached a balanced agreement on 14 february. the compromise agreement, which amends the commission's initial proposal, was reached in a record time of two weeks, was approved by the majority of member states and was reconfirmed in the committee on legal affairs. and now the plenary of the european parliament has the floor. the european union introduced the supplementary protection certificate to bring and promote research in europe. approximately half of the patent life of a new treatment is lost during the research, development and regulatory processes, and the certificate helped to restore part of that patent life. but the market has evolved, ladies and gentlemen, and generics manufactured within europe have been left defenseless because, during the period of the patent and during this additional period of protection, they could neither produce nor store the protected products, even when it is exclusively for export to third countries where protection does not exist or has expired. meanwhile, in other third countries which do not have this additional period, they can do so. this means that generic producers who choose to manufacture outside europe have a competitive advantage in the rest of the world and, moreover, their products will enter our market before european generics. the innovative industry, ladies and gentlemen, is key in europe and when we talk about the strategy for europe we must inexcusably continue to defend a knowledge-based economy. let's not forget that this part of our industry invests approximately 35 billion euros in r&amp;d in europe, approves thousands of drugs and new active ingredients every year, so it's clear that our system of intellectual property incentives exists, is working to manufacture and deliver new, improved treatments to the patients who need them. but the generic biopharmaceutical industry must play a key role in europe's export performance and be one of the most competitive pillars of the union's economy, helping to restore european growth. the certificate exception is an effort to level the playing field between generic manufacturers in the union and in third countries. from now on, ladies and gentlemen, manufacturers of generics and biosimilars established in the union will be able to manufacture these products for export to third country markets where this protection does not exist or has expired, thereby helping those manufacturers to compete effectively on third country markets. this regulation will also allow these same manufacturers established in the union to store the products in the member state where they have been manufactured during the last six months of protection. the purpose is to enter the market of any member state after the expiry of the certificate, thereby helping to compete effectively in the union immediately after the expiry of the protection. we have included appropriate safeguards to not weaken our commitment to intellectual property and innovation. in this respect, manufacturers of generic and biosimilar medicinal products will be required to publish and send information to the holder of the spc, to prevent the industry from circumventing the rules of the exception, and at least three months in advance. the notification will ensure the transparency of the system and increase competition on european markets, but at the same time the regulation respects the maintenance of the confidentiality of particularly sensitive information. the adoption of this regulation will be of great benefit to the european industry and to pharmaceutical savings. the commission has estimated that by 2025 this will mean an increase in production of between eur 7.3 and 9.5 billion and the creation of between 20 000 and 25 000 jobs in the union, as well as savings in pharmaceutical expenditure of up to 4%. ladies and gentlemen, this report has not been easy. we all had to make an effort to understand the different positions until we reached a balance and a consensus. i would like to thank the speakers on the other side of the house and our collaborators who have worked so hard. i would especially like to remember my collaborator, mercedes, who worked very hard. i thank the romanian presidency for standing up to a great issue.

mr president, commissioner avramopoulos, you know that it has been a great honour to have worked for many years on the dossier, on the legislative issue, on european law - nothing less than the european visa regulation, the new european visa code, which is returning to this european parliament for final debate and vote. we have completed years of hard work, in which i have to thank, as is customary in this parliament, the alternative rapporteurs, who have cooperated effectively and loyally in the conduct of this european law; and, of course, you yourself, commissioner avramopoulos, for your punctual follow-up and your dedication to the legislative affairs of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs. we have listened intently at various seminars and hearings - the parliamentary hearings we practise in committee - to the so-called stakeholders - the representatives of legitimate interests - on this great legislative issue, which fulfils a major objective of the area of freedom, justice and security that we were talking about a minute ago when we were discussing the european border and coast guard: an integrated management of the union's external borders that ensures the free movement of persons within the european union, but at the same time provides the necessary legislative instruments to harmonise the conditions for authorisation to enter the european union. entry also for lawful and legitimate purposes: what we call 'good faith travellers', people who come for short stays - between 90 and 180 days maximum - for tourism, business, artistic activities, sports, study or research. and all these situations have been covered in this european regulation on visas after a very detailed work of integrating all the amendments and positions that have been heard. we have finally achieved a reasonable balance in order to ensure the same conditions for authorizing access to the territory of the european union, visa fees - and therefore the price for obtaining entry authorization - application forms, list of documents supporting entry... and of course i have tried, against all odds, to preserve the objective that was at stake: better facilitation, easier access to the european union for the bona fide traveller, for the bona fide entrant. and this is important, particularly considering that i come from a country which receives millions and millions and millions of tourists a year; i come from a community, an outermost region - the canaries - which receives 18 million tourists a year and therefore it is extremely important to maintain the purpose of facilitating entry, access to the schengen area. some of the amendments we have managed to balance in the final text of the law are those relating to the visa fee: between 60 and 80 euros to adapt it to the real costs, with a reduction for those under 18, for those under 6, and with exceptions for students, researchers and also artists and sportsmen. we have established a commitment on health insurance for the commission to review within 15 months of the entry into force of the new european law, and we have also established a reasonable balance of interests on the deadlines for obtaining visas, so that it is easier and also cheaper, taking into account that buying airline tickets well in advance facilitates access to the european union for people who apply for visas well in advance. but finally i would like to refer to the importance of preserving facilitation over the safety-focused approach, because there has been a contamination of the access of bona fide travellers to the european union with the fight against irregular immigration and against terrorism, which has nothing to do with access for lawful purposes to the european union. finally, in the face of the attempt to impose a mechanical link with the return of irregular immigrants, we have struck a balance, so that the category of positive incentives to third countries cooperating in the prevention of irregular immigration has been established, so that european law is as well received as possible by the member states.
i would like to congratulate mr juan fernando. the establishment of a common visa regime is not only relevant to security and the prevention of irregular immigration but is also essential for the proper functioning of many important economic sectors. for example, tourism, which is of particular importance for many regions of europe. in 2017 alone, almost 14 million short-stay schengen visas were issued. more flexible procedures, such as electronic processing with up to six months' notice for applications, the possibility to apply for multiple-entry visas with extended validity, the allocation of more resources to strengthen security or improved cooperation on readmission are some of the improvements in visa policy. the agreed changes will boost tourism, trade and business, while enhancing security and reducing the risks of illegal exploitation. it is essential that any improvements to the common visa policy be made in accordance with the specifications required by the sis and the vis in order to facilitate the implementation of interoperability in the information systems. mr. president, i'm leaving too. it's 35 years of public life that i want to sum up in one word: thank you. or two, thank you very much. see you around. and thank you, from the bottom of my heart.

the rights of workers, creditors and shareholders. the new harmonised procedures therefore also include the safeguards necessary to protect the rights of all. this directive, ladies and gentlemen, is based on the need to respond to the evolution of the case law of the european court of justice on the freedom of establishment, enshrined in article 49 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union. we have always advocated that companies established in one member state should have the right and freedom to move their headquarters to another without losing their legal personality. this right, ladies and gentlemen, can be exercised even if the company does not carry on any economic activity in the host state. however, we also believe, as does the rapporteur and the council, that it market unit. i therefore personally emphasized, as the rapporteur knows, that companies should have to justify, among other things, whether they had received public aid, since we see every day cases our priority, because we want a united europe without frontiers, and it is our responsibility to ensure that.
author. mr president, i should like to begin by saying that this is not so much an oral question at the end of the legislature as a political complaint which this parliament wishes to make to the council and the commission. and it is a political complaint about what we consider to be a lack of loyal cooperation, a lack of institutional cooperation between the council, the commission and parliament, which i think is very serious. to begin by recalling the facts, i have to say that article 226 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union already gave the european parliament the legislative initiative to regulate the powers of the committees of inquiry in 2009, when the treaty of lisbon was adopted. i would remind you that the european parliament has only legislative initiative in two areas: the european electoral law and the regulation of committees of inquiry. the text was already adopted in 2012 - three years later - with david martin as rapporteur, who started negotiations with the council and the commission in the previous legislature; no agreement was reached and in 2014 the text was adopted at first reading, albeit without the agreement of the commission and the council. when i was appointed rapporteur at the beginning of this term, in 2015, i started trying to negotiate with the council and the commission a text that would be approved by all three institutions. and the fact is, ladies and gentlemen - president-in-office of the council. – mr president, as we approach the end of the term, it is indeed an appropriate moment to discuss the important issue of the exercise, of its inquiry powers by the european parliament, and take stock of recent events. let me start by assuring you that the council has always shared the view that committees of inquiry are an important instrument, allowing the european parliament to exercise political control in a union founded on the values of respect for democracy and the rule of law, as required by the treaty. since the martin report in 2011, the council has been examining a series of proposals in a very constructive spirit and in the respect of its duty of sincere cooperation. however, as is well known, the martin report raised serious legal and institutional concerns in the council and in the commission with regard to the limits imposed by article 226 of the treaty. indeed, this proposal for so far-reaching an extension of the rights of committees of inquiry was considered contrary to article 226. despite subsequent efforts to reconcile the diverse positions, such as the more recent work by the experts of the three legal services at technical level which held so many meetings, the progress made on some less problematic provisions resulting from this work did not match and did not solve the most complex issues of a legal and political nature. as was stated in a letter sent to ms hübner on 25 october last year by the austrian presidency, the council therefore welcomed the non-paper prepared by the rapporteur, mr jáuregui atondo, representing a new attempt to revive the political dialogue among the three institutions. the non-paper indeed contains a number of improvements compared to the proposal of 2014. it meets some of the concerns expressed by the council on previous occasions and takes up some of the solutions which are jointly suggested by the legal experts of the three institutions. however, the non-paper still contains a number of provisions which give rise to serious legal and political concerns for the council, which were raised on many past occasions. in substance, the council’s position on these fundamental issues has not changed since the martin report, and to be more specific, let me mention, among the most problematic issues, this power to summon individuals who are not officials as witnesses and to enforce such a measure by sanctions; the hearing of officials and other servants of the union as witnesses; the power to request documents from natural or legal persons who have no role in the implementation of union law; and the imposition of sanctions in the event of non-compliance. and finally, the provisions on sanctions. let me recall that criminal law in the rules on criminal procedure are matters for which the member states are responsible. the competences of the union in that field are very limited. i will not go into more detail here, as you are, i hope, very familiar with the council’s concerns, which i explained in a detailed manner in the letter i have already mentioned. since the beginning of its term, the romanian presidency has been ready to continue to clarify the respective positions, also in the commission, building upon the austrian presidency’s engagement in the many informal contacts between our predecessors and mr jáuregui and mrs hübner. i can assure you that the council continues to be open to a constructive dialogue with the european parliament in order to explore ways forward on this legally and politically-complex file. should the new parliament wish to carry on the work based on the progress made so far, the council stands ready to do so in full respect of its duty of sincere cooperation.
member of the commission. – mr president, let me first welcome this occasion offered by this oral question to set out the commission’s positions regarding the proposal for the regulation on the european parliament’s right of inquiry. while it is of course for the parliament to make a proposal, the procedure also requires the consent of the council and of the commission. since the entry into force of the lisbon treaty, the european parliament has made several proposals for such a regulation. the latest informal proposal, in the form of a non-paper proposal, was politically endorsed by the committee on constitutional affairs in april last year and transmitted to the commission and to the council in may last year. the commission acknowledges that the new informal proposal is drafted in more precise legal terms and incorporates several improvements: for instance, as regards the rules on the setting-up of the committee of inquiry, the procedural rules applying to its investigation or the introduction of a central contact point for inquiry. the new informal proposal also contains references to the regulation on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data by eu institutions, and to the framework agreement between the european parliament and the european commission. however, the non-paper proposal still contains a number of legal and institutional concerns that have been at the heart of this discussion with the parliament and the council since 2012. the most important concerns are: sanctions for non-compliance with the provisions of the regulations; certain aspects of the investigative means which would be in the hands of the committee, such as on-the-spot investigations, hearings of commissioners and former commissioners, hearings of officials and former officials, as well as hearings of natural persons; the newly introduced rule regarding remedies in the case of violation of the provisions of the regulation by a committee of inquiry, its members and officials and other servants of the european parliament; and last, provisions which seem to grant discretionary power to the parliament with regard to the suspension of the committee proceedings during the related court procedure. notwithstanding these concerns, i would like to stress the commission’s continued willingness and commitment to engage in a constructive trilateral discussion, with a view to finding appropriate solutions to the divergences that still exist between the three institutions. the future regulation of the right of inquiry should provide the european parliament with the appropriate instrument to fully respect institutional prerogatives and the relevant legal frameworks of the member states.

in writing. – the critique of so-called humanitarian assistance in the flows of illegal immigration across the mediterranean has been made suspect because it is being used by populist governments and movements to justify their hard, anti-immigration stance. but the critique remains valid and needs a response. sea projects originating and financed from outside the mediterranean are serving to encourage people traffickers and migrants who would not otherwise attempt very dangerous crossings to multiply their activities. these ‘humanitarian’ entrepreneurs are subject to no proper regulation and basically engage in a catch-as-catch-can game with approaching migrant boats. the situation is not sustainable for political, security, economic and social reasons. yet europe still does not have a functioning policy to process legal migration, dublin ii arrangements remain unfair and outdated, schengen procedures could soon be placed under new pressure and the feeding of false hopes to arriving migrants is serving to strengthen the reach of people traffickers. so, in my view, uncritical support of projects of humanitarian assistance in the mediterranean will, while the other chapters of european immigration are still pending, serve to provoke further political and moral crises in the medium term. this needs to be reconsidered.
the next item on the agenda is the following: council and commission statements on the clean air zone in european union cities (2019/2738 (rsp)).
president-in-office of the council. – mr president, air pollution directly causes both chronic and serious diseases such as asthma, cardiovascular problems and lung cancer. ill health caused by air pollution costs the economy billions of euros in lost working days and causes 400 000 premature deaths per year in europe alone. that is why air quality has been, and is, an extremely important issue for the council. the eu has for some time already had a solid legal framework in place that includes the ambient air quality directives and is the basis for measures taken at national, regional and local levels. low emission zones and incentives for cleaner transportation modes have been successfully implemented in different cities and regions in europe with encouraging results. the data show that air quality has improved across europe over the past decades, in particular in urban areas, as emissions of many pollutants have been successfully reduced. in this context, let me highlight the decisive actions taken by the co—legislators over the last few months to strengthen the array of eu legislative instruments in this area even more. i think we can look with satisfaction at the results achieved with the outgoing parliament on a number of new legislative measures that provide, directly and indirectly, important contributions to cleaner air. the clean vehicles directive promotes the market uptake of zero and low-emission vehicles by introducing binding minimum targets for their use in public procurement in each member state. these measures will play a key role in cutting greenhouse gas and air pollutant emissions and will also contribute – to an important extent – to achieving the eu’s climate commitments under the paris agreement. the directive overhauling electronic tolling systems in the eu updates the technical interoperability requirements for such systems. it will create a system of exchange of information to reach foreign drivers who have not paid their road charges and fees with a view to enforcing the respect of road tolls more efficiently. at this stage it also covers charges for access to urban areas, but not complete bans or limitations to certain types of vehicles. however, the review clause of the directive requests that, by 2023, the commission evaluates the extension of the directive to cover low emission zones, restricted access zones and other urban vehicle access regulation schemes. finally, let me also mention the recently adapted climate legislation to reduce co2 emissions from cars, vans and heavy—duty vehicles that will accelerate the uptake of cleaner technologies such as zero and low-emission vehicles, thereby also helping to reduce air pollution in our cities. the finnish presidency attaches great importance to the protection of air quality and to improving the environmental performance of vehicles. in this context, the presidency considers that it’s crucial to continue the mandatory application of real driving emissions test procedures on the road and not to rely solely on test procedures in laboratory conditions. to reach that goal, the parliament and the council need to come to an agreement on conformity factors. as you know, the devices we use to measure real driving emissions have technical uncertainties. conformity factors take account of these uncertainties. we hope to reach a swift agreement with parliament on the new real driving emissions (rde) proposal in order to ensure legal certainty for all parties involved. it is of the utmost importance to ensure the implementation of eu air quality standards by all stakeholders, an issue that is closely followed by the commission. we know that there are still compliance gaps for some key pollutants. the council is therefore looking forward to the completion of the commission’s fitness check of the ambient air quality directives, which it will examine with great interest as soon as available. good air quality, especially in cities, has a positive impact on the quality of life for each of us. a number of cities in the eu still exceeded the limit values of the national emission ceilings directive. thus we all have to work nationally to secure better health for our citizens. the strong link between air quality and climate change means that similar measures can help to tackle both. for example, the transport sector is the biggest source of emissions of black carbon that accelerates the warming of the arctic region. this is important to keep in mind in the eu discussions as well. thank you very much for your attention.
member of the commission. – mr president, clean air, and protecting the health of our citizens, is a key priority for the commission. the fact that air pollution causes over 400 000 premature deaths every year is unacceptable. we have to act, to the benefit of our citizens. and that is precisely what this commission has been doing this mandate – and we have done so resolutely. our actions have been based on three main pillars. first: supporting our member states in reaching eu air quality standards. we have made eu funding available under various financial streams and the member states have successfully used that funding to address the air quality challenge. to cite just one figure: in the current programming period 2014-2020, almost eur two billion have been directly allocated to air quality measures under the european structural and investment funds. second point: improving how we regulate emissions at their source. prominent examples for this are the directive regulating medium combustion plants and the package of real driving emissions rules. third and final: taking decisive enforcement action when and where exceedances of air quality limit values persist. the commission is currently pursuing 30 infringement procedures against 20 member states for exceedances of particulate matter, nitrogen dioxide or sulphur dioxide limit values. for two cases already, the court of justice has confirmed that member states need to accelerate their efforts to improve air quality further. the commission is doing its part, and will continue to do so as the measures taken so far have resulted in some improvements. but we also need to remember what that part is. our legislation on ambient air sets limit values on air pollution, and an obligation to keep exceedance periods as short as possible, and the commission steps in when and where this is not the case. but the choice of measures lies with member states. it is up to their authorities, across levels of governance, being national or local, to define which coordinated measures they take to meet the agreed limit values. when the commission takes infringement action against member states, the goal is not to ensure that one measure or the other is implemented – be it a specific clean air zone, support for renewing the fleet, replacing old boilers in households, or any other measure. the goal is, first and foremost, to speed up efforts in those member states to reach compliance with eu legislation, and to keep any period of exceedance as short as possible. beyond legislation and infringements, we support cities in a number of ways to make their air cleaner. when it comes to urban mobility, for example, we are working with national and local authorities to identify best practices on urban vehicle access regulation schemes such as low-emission zones and traffic restriction measures, but also to foster consistency in line with single market principles and ensure information on such access regulations.

mr president, we are becoming increasingly aware of the extent of the ecological crisis we are facing, and it is not because of politicians or european leaders - as we are seeing - but because of organised civil society, especially young people. four hundred thousand people in europe, ten thousand in spain and fourteen in madrid alone die prematurely every day from air pollution. in central madrid, this pollution has been reduced drastically. and it is a shame - it is a shame - that conservative governments, who have systematically flouted environmental legislation, now want to reverse it. the european union must prevent this. we must be brave. we must respond to the demands of the millions of citizens who are calling for changes in environmental policies. we cannot allow this to be reversed for purely sectarian reasons. we may think differently, but we breathe the same.
mr president, if only the cities were in the countryside! at least that's what many people think. a recent survey of european citizens revealed that people in large cities would like three things: less traffic, more green space and cleaner air. they also believe that it is up to politicians to take action to tackle air pollution in large cities. every city dweller would lose a year of healthy life because of air pollution. a year of life! well, yes, it is our responsibility, ladies and gentlemen, to take this into account and to fight against all pollution, and in particular air pollution. we need to put in place effective measures, first toughening up standards for fine particulate matter, then supporting clean air zones initiatives that are protected from heavy and polluting road traffic, promoting the installation of well insulated buildings with high-performance heating technologies and finally helping the most disadvantaged people to get better heating.
